10592-adventures-in-friendship:
David Grayson, writing from a farm in the American countryside, made Adventures in Friendship from short essays about neighbors, visitors, and daily life. The book opens with a salesman who greets him like a brother because of lodge badges, then wonders what real fellowship means when it is not bought by membership. Grayson's voice is warm, plain, and gently humorous.

Later chapters follow other small adventures: talks on the road, kindnesses exchanged, and lessons learned from ordinary people. The theme throughout is that friendship grows from attention and honesty, not from clubs or ceremony. Readers looking for quiet, thoughtful essays on getting along with others will find this book easy company.
10865-play-making-a-manual-of-craftsmans:
William Archer published Play-Making in 1912 as a manual of craftsmanship for dramatists. Archer stresses that the book is essentially new, though short passages from older articles are embedded in it. He draws examples from published plays readers can check, turning often to Shakespeare and Ibsen as the most accessible playwrights.

More than half the chapters were written on shipboard and in places with few books at hand, yet the manual is thorough on plot, character, and dialogue. Archer's advice is practical, not theoretical. Aspiring playwrights get a classic guide, still respected for its clarity about how plays are built.
11045-the-ghost-ship:
Richard Middleton collected ghost stories in this volume, most first printed in The Century, English Review, Vanity Fair, and The Academy. The title story is told by a Fairfield villager, who calls his home the ghostiest place in England. Ghosts of lads who died in war keep tryst with lasses in the churchyard on Saturday nights.

Middleton's narrator insists that spirits stay where they are left alone, and that Londoners, curious and interfering, would drive them away. Other stories follow authors, critics, and villagers meeting the uncanny in quiet English settings. The collection charms through its dry humour and its belief that the supernatural belongs to ordinary places, accepted without fuss.
12730-the-high-school-boys-fishing-trip:
Dick and Co. head for the wilderness in this Gridley fishing tale, and find mystery along with trout. A strange packing box, left as a gift for Dick as trustee, sets off a hunt for its sender, while a haunting face and a captured camp deepen the puzzle. Rival boys Dodge and Bayless hover near the trouble.

The trip mixes camp life, a wild ride to safety, and a secret Tom Reade finally tells. Hancock keeps the tone light even when powder mills and night alarms loom. Young readers get outdoor fun with a detective thread, ending in the friends' usual loyal, laughing close.
12954-the-phantom-ship:
Captain Frederick Marryat's Phantom Ship, most notable of his three novels on a historic basis, tells of Philip Vanderdecken and the Flying Dutchman legend. Unlike its predecessor Snarleyyow, its ghosts are never explained away, and diablerie drives the romance in earnest, melodramatic spirit. Marryat's sea experience gives old Dutch seamanship a lifelike air.

A homecoming scene shows Father Mathias struggling to keep pace with Philip's strides, urging him to check joyful hopes lest disappointment crush them, as Flushing lies a quarter mile ahead. The novel blends sea adventure with supernatural dread. It remains Marryat's finest ghostly romance.
15381-victorian-short-stories-stories-of:
This volume gathers five Victorian short stories, all on courtship, by five different writers. William Schwenk Gilbert opens with Angela, an inverted love story told by a paralyzed man in a small room above a Venetian canal. He lives on thirty pounds a year, painting flowers and fruit in watercolor, with only a deaf old woman to tend him.

The other tales widen the theme. Anthony Trollope writes of a parson's daughter at Oxney Colne, Hubert Crackanthorpe of Anthony Garstin's courtship, George Egerton of a little grey glove, and Israel Zangwill of a woman beater. Love here is rarely smooth: money, pride, violence, and social rank all stand in the way. The set shows Victorian fiction testing how courtship really worked, beyond the romance of the wedding day.
1551-a-cathedral-courtship:
Kate Douglas Wiggin's Cathedral Courtship, first published in 1893 with illustrations by Clifford Carleton, follows an American girl touring English cathedrals who finds romance among choirs, cloisters, and close quarters. The courtship unfolds through cathedral towns, with humour, sentiment, and a traveller's eye for old stones.

Wiggin writes lightly and warmly, and the cathedral setting gives the love story a picturesque frame. The book went through many editions in its first year. It is a charming period romance for readers who love England, churches, and a gentle love story. The cathedral towns give the romance a lovely backdrop.
16273-the-manual-of-heraldry-fifth-editi:
The Manual of Heraldry, in a fifth edition from Arthur Hall in London, offers a concise description of every term used in the science, with a dictionary of every designation. Four hundred engravings on wood illustrate shields, charges, crowns, and coats, making the book useful at a glance. A transcriber's note records small spelling fixes, such as scarpe for scrape and seme forms in the dictionary.

Heraldry's language of blazon, tinctures, and bearings can baffle beginners, and this manual aims to make it plain and searchable. Antiquaries, artists, and family historians used such guides to read tombs, seals, and windows. The book remains a handy reference for anyone decoding a coat of arms.
16455-the-otterbein-hymnal-for-use-in-pu:
Edmund S. Lorenz prepared this hymnal for the Church of the United Brethren in Christ, ordered by its 1886 General Conference and issued in Dayton in 1892. Hymns are grouped by theme: praise, sanctuary, Sabbath, morning and evening, the Holy Spirit, sin and atonement, and the Christian life in all its stages. Later sections cover prayer, affliction, and faith.

The book was made for both church services and home singing, small enough for general use. Its order moves from worship through the life of Christ to the believer's daily walk. For historians of American hymnody, it shows what a late nineteenth-century congregation actually sang.
16921-plague-ship:
Andre Norton, writing as Andrew North, wrote this 1956 science fiction novel Plague Ship, copyright 1956. It opens on the Solar Queen, a Galactic Free Trader of Terra registry. Dane Thorson, cargo-master apprentice, stands in a cramped bather. Rip Shannon, assistant astrogator, rubs highly scented paste between his shoulder blades. The cabin reeks of spice, and Rip jokes that Dane will be the best-smelling Terran ever to set boot on Sargol.

Norton sends a free trader crew to Sargol, where talkative Salariki must be heard out before a straight answer comes. Trade, aliens, and a plague threat drive the tale. Readers who like classic space adventure will find a brisk, young-adult novel of a working starship crew, full of alien customs and frontier trade.
17266-the-banner-boy-scouts-or-the-strug:
George A. Warren's 1912 Banner Boy Scouts, or the Struggle for Leadership, opens with a roll call in a barn. Paul's troop must stay quiet, for Ted Slavin's rival crowd is out hunting them, and Bluff Shipley's stammer marks the fun. Chapters follow the disappearing coins, the first scout leader, a coward checked, Peleg's trap, the rival troops, a fire test, and a camp in the woods.

Warren writes in brisk boys'-book style, with pluck, woodcraft, and fair play at its heart. The Stanhope troop's road to the honor brand closes the tale. Young readers who like scout stories will enjoy a sturdy, old-style adventure of leadership earned, not claimed.
17414-the-blood-ship:
Norman Springer's 1922 Blood Ship opens with a writing man who talks so much that Captain Shreve spins his yarn just to shut him up. The passenger, weak of lung and hunting mild tropical breezes, seeks local color and news of King Waldon, the island trader dead in Samoa. Waldon sailed into a Samoan harbor in an open boat with only his beautiful young wife, and the captain knew him.

From that frame grows a South Seas tale of a cargo carrier, a vanished viking, and a romantic legend too good not to put in a book. Springer writes in salty, seafaring prose, with humor and mystery in turn. Readers who like sea yarns will enjoy a lively novel of the islands, their traders, and their ghosts.
19487-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
A. Hugh Fisher wrote this guide to Hereford Cathedral for Bell's cathedral series, published in London in the late eighteen hundreds. It traces the building's history, then walks the reader round its outside and through its inside, with a brief history of the bishop's see to close.

Old inscriptions get room here, including a bequest that freed travelers from tolls and a wife's proud approval of her husband's gift. Made for visitors who want sound facts in plain words, the guide still serves anyone walking Hereford's nave with open eyes.
19881-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Bell's Cathedrals was a series of small guides to great English churches. This volume, by C. King Eley, describes Carlisle Cathedral's fabric. It adds a brief history of the episcopal see. The aim is a work both scholarly and usable. A student of archaeology should find it sound. An ordinary visitor or tourist should find it plain enough. That double audience shaped the whole series.

Carlisle's cathedral stands near the Scottish border, scarred by border wars. Its choir is among England's finest medieval works. A compact guide had to carry architecture and history together. Bell's series filled travelers' pockets across Britain. Eley's volume shows the formula working well. It is Edwardian heritage writing at its most useful.
20280-the-hill-a-romance-of-friendship:
Horace Annesley Vachell wrote The Hill, a romance of friendship at an English public school. Vachell assures a friend that boys like Verney and Scaife truly exist. No one knows that better than the friend himself, he writes. Chapters promise self-questioning, sacrifice, and a final good night.

The Hill opens with five hundred strange faces before a new boy. Life lies in front of him, and home behind, as he arrives. School tales of this era prize loyalty, games, and unspoken codes. Readers get a fond, serious portrait of friendship formed under school rules.
20651-a-jolly-fellowship:
Frank R. Stockton's A Jolly Fellowship, published in 1880, is a boys' adventure told by one of the boys himself. The narrator saw for himself everything worth seeing in the events he relates. He trusts his own eyes more than hearsay, and says so proudly at the start.

Will is a good-looking boy, with brown hair and gray eyes. He and his friend set out on travels that carry them far from home, into mishaps and discoveries. Stockton, soon famous for The Lady, or the Tiger?, writes here with the same dry fun, sized for young readers on the road.
20861-friendship:
Chasing friendship for gain is like chasing a rainbow's end for gold, says Friendship, from 1898. A true friend proves useful in the highest sense, the essay grants. Yet friends must never be billed like members of a dues club.

Hugh Black, a Scottish preacher, wrote this famed essay book on friendship's worth. He treats choice, keeping, and the joys and duties of true bonds. His warm, wise tone won readers on both sides of the Atlantic. The book stays in print in spirit, still quoted where friendship's deep value needs plain, kind words.
21067-overdue-the-story-of-a-missing-shi:
Clipper ships stood at their peak when Harry Collingwood set this tale of a missing ship, in the days before steamers ruled the seas. A seventeen-year-old midshipman of the Salamis is suddenly ordered aboard the Mercury, an emigrant ship found drifting in mid-ocean. All her officers have died in separate accidents.

The bosun and carpenter left aboard cannot navigate, so the boy must take command himself. For a while the ship runs well under his orders, until fresh trouble strikes. Collingwood, trained as a naval architect, writes the sails and deck work with authority, and sea humour runs through the danger.
21382-son-philip:
Philip Hexton, the hero of George Manville Fenn's novel Son Philip, is the son of an old mine owner. His parents hope he will choose a safer trade, but Philip wants only one job. He means to work as an overseer in the family mine, down among the men.

Under Philip the mine starts to run well, yet some miners break his safety rules on purpose. They smoke where gas may gather, and one man swears he will leave his mark on Philip. The story builds through tense scenes underground, escapes, and hard choices about duty. It ends with Philip running a mine that is both sound and safe.
21573-the-phantom-ship:
Captain Marryat retells the legend of the Flying Dutchman in The Phantom Ship, published in 1839, his thirteenth book. The tale opens in the mid-seventeenth century, on the edge of a small Dutch town. A cottage by a moat, with a narrow bridged crossing, sets the scene.

Philip Vanderdecken sails to free his father, doomed to beat round the Cape forever. A sacred relic, a loved wife, and dark powers bar his way. Judges have called the book one of Marryat's very best. Sea craft and ghost lore blend here in a way no writer has matched since.
21745-the-life-of-a-ship:
A small boy named Davy watches a new sailing ship take shape in a shipyard in this Ballantyne story for young readers. The vessel is the Fair Nancy, and her life from launch to wreck gives the book its plan. Davy is at last allowed to sail in her as a boy seaman. He is seasick first, then learns the rigging and the sails.

Storms strike hard: a hurricane knocks the ship over and her boats are lost. A raft saves a few, and a rope swum ashore saves the rest on a hostile coast. The crew walks out to a village and finds its way home by Quebec. The tale teaches how a ship lives and dies.
22107-wood-carving-design-and-workmanshi:
George Jack, a leading figure in the Arts and Crafts movement, wrote Wood Carving: Design and Workmanship. Jack had examined the methods used in working shops across the trade. He set aside vain survivals, the habits kept only because they were old. His aim is a standard of quality for craft work joined to design.

The book treats design as part of workmanship, not decoration added later. Tools, timber, pattern, and the carver's training all come under review. Jack wrote for students in the new art schools and for working carvers alike. His volume belongs to the movement that tried to save hand skill from the factory, and it still guides carvers today.
22541-the-misplaced-battleship:
The Misplaced Battleship is a comic science fiction story with a huge ship. Its narrator confirms a guess about the vessel late at night. It is a late Empire battleship of the Warlord class.

Undoubtedly, he says, it is a most efficient engine of destruction. Over a half mile of defensive screens and armament fill her. She could probably turn any existing fleet into radioactive ash. Misplacing such a ship is thus more than a clerical error. The story mines that absurd gap for humor and trouble. Bureaucracy meets doomsday hardware in its pages with dry effect. Readers get space opera played for laughs, in Harry Harrison's vein.
22652-a-campfire-girl-s-test-of-friendsh:
Jane L. Stewart wrote A Camp Fire Girl's Test of Friendship, a girls' series novel built around the Camp Fire Girls, the outdoor organization founded just before the First World War. The catalog record gives no year. Stewart's heroines camp, work, and face small trials of loyalty under the movement's ideals of health and helpfulness.

In the sample, Bessie looks back on a stay nearly spoiled by the girls in the camp next door. If those girls had had their way, she says, the troop would have kept not one pleasant memory of the place. Rivalry between camps, and friendship tested inside the troop, drive the plot. Such books taught outdoor skills inside a story, and they preserve the hopes adults held for girls of the era.
23111-riley-songs-of-friendship:
James Whitcomb Riley thanks his readers in Riley Songs of Friendship, dated 1885 in this edition. Riley addresses friends whose kindness reaches him only in ink and pen. Could he ever tell them the good they do him, he writes, speech would fail him into baby talk, his warmed blood laughing through his veins.

Riley, Indiana's Hoosier poet, built a national audience on dialect verse and sentiment, and friendship was his home subject. The songs gathered here trade in letters, reunions, and old neighbors remembered kindly. His lines were built for recitation, warm in the mouth and easy to memorize. Modern readers meet a poet America once knew by heart, preserved in one of his gentlest collections.
23154-the-hill-a-romance-of-friendship:
A platform farewell opens The Hill, a romance of friendship. A man and a boy pace a long station platform in silence. The boy wonders at his uncle's strange quiet. Then the elder John Verney stops, sets both hands on young John's shoulders, and looks down into eyes as grey and steady as his own.

Horace Annesley Vachell, to whom this school novel is credited, sets the boy's story at Harrow, on the hill of its title. Friendship between schoolboys, tested by honor, games, and loss, forms the book's famous core. A generation of readers wept over its central bond. Vachell wrote from inside the public-school world he depicts. The platform scene, an uncle's silence before a first term, tells new readers exactly what weather to expect.
24407-the-italian-cook-book-the-art-of-e:
Mrs. Maria Gentile compiled this Italian cook book, published by the Italian Book Company in 1919. Its subtitle promises the art of eating well, with practical recipes of the Italian cuisine, pastries, sweets, frozen delicacies, and syrups. The book opens with broth, or soup stock, the basis of nearly all Italian soups. Good broth puts meat in cold water and boils it slowly, with bones and soup greens: celery, carrots, and parsley.

Sugar browned at the fire and diluted in cold water browns the broth, and though broth has little nutritive power, it promotes digestion. A substantial broth for invalids cuts beef thin, covers it with cold water and salt, and seals the pan. It stays on a low fire six hours, then on a strong fire ten minutes. Soup of cappelletti, little hats, follows, with paste of eggs, flour, and salt. Readers get Italian cooking, plainly taught.
24576-an-interpretation-of-friends-worsh:
N. Jean Toomer wrote this short guide to Friends worship, published by the Friends General Conference at Philadelphia in 1947 at twenty-five cents. Its chapters cover worship and love, the basis of Friends worship and other inward practices, what to do in the meeting for worship, and questions and answers.

Toomer writes that worship is the action of the spirit, springing from our depths as love does. She explains silent meeting, inward prayer, and the place of ministry for newcomers. The guide is brief, plain, and welcoming. Readers curious about Quaker worship will find it a gentle and practical introduction.
24985-comedies-of-courtship:
Anthony Hope's 1896 collection, published by Charles Scribner's Sons, gathers six comedies of courtship. They are The Wheel of Love, The Lady of the Pool, The Curate of Poltons, A Three-Volume Novel, The Philosopher in the Apple Orchard, and The Decree of Duke Deodonato. Hope notes that four stories had already appeared without his consent, their titles changed beyond recognition, in a small American volume; here they appear in proper form by his authority.

The Wheel of Love opens on plighted lovers who should be happy: young, healthy, well off, with house, horses, river, and a weekly box from Mudie's. John stays with Miss Bussey to delight his fiancée Mary Travers, yet Mary sits sadly fingering a letter in her waistband while John strides moodily on the gravel. At dinner the party's cross-currents show: Charlie Ellerton's labored attentiveness to Mary, Miss Bussey's puzzled gravity, and Laing's calculating eye.
25493-a-cathedral-courtship:
Kate Douglas Wiggin tells a light romance that unfolds among English cathedrals, illustrated by Charles E. Brock. A young woman's tour of great churches supplies the setting, the company, and the slow chances for talk, misunderstanding, and growing affection that carry a courtship plot.

Wiggin, already known for Penelope's English, Irish, and Scottish experiences, writes in the same warm, observant voice here. Cathedral stone, music, and daily travel give the love story its shape, while humour keeps the sentiment from turning heavy. The Penelope books listed at the front show the same taste for travel talk and light comedy, now turned to a new romance.
26194-the-grain-ship:
Morgan Robertson's volume gathers ten sea and adventure stories first printed in magazines such as Harper's Monthly, The Smart Set, and The Popular Magazine. The title story opens in a restaurant. A white-haired commodore tells of a tight merchant ship found sailing the Bay of Biscay under topsails. She was deserted, with stores and water intact, yet her deck was covered with dead rats.

Other tales include From the Darkness and the Depths, Noah's Ark, The Finishing Touch, The Rock, and Extracts from Noah's Log. A later story strands a mate and a narrator at odds, armed against maddened sailors. Robertson, a lifelong student of nautical life, writes with salt-water detail and a taste for mystery at sea.
3005-tom-swift-and-his-airship:
Victor Appleton wrote Tom Swift and His Airship as a boys' adventure about a young inventor and his dirigible, the Red Cloud. Tom and Mr. Sharp build and test the craft, surviving an explosion, a collision with a tower, and a scramble off a roof. Andy tries a trick, a runaway auto causes trouble, and a prize gives the boys a goal.

The airship rises higher and higher, darts like a bird in huge circles, and comes to rest in the air when the gas machine fills its container. Later chapters bring a robbery charge, a wreck, a sheriff aboard, and a raid on a criminal camp. The book remains a brisk example of early science fiction for young readers, full of machines and chases.
30375-the-conflict-between-private-monop:
John Graham Brooks delivers a Weinstock Lecture on the morals of trade, published in December 1909 by Houghton Mifflin. As president of the National Consumers' League, he asks how private monopoly bears on good citizenship and on business life under a new economic order.

Brooks places the lecture in a series on moral law and trade, first given at the University of California, with companion talks on commercialism, journalism, and business in public life. He argues from the standpoint of consumers and citizens, not firms alone, weighing profit against public duty. The short book remains a clear statement of Progressive Era concern over concentrated power.
30379-field-trip:
Gene Hunter writes a time-travel story in which Kial, disgusted with a slow, cumbersome train, tries to learn the ways of strange creatures who are his ancestors. Lonely in a backward age, he spots a fellow being in the same carriage and hastens to introduce himself.

The stranger gives his origin as 8000, from the seventh galaxy, while Kial calls himself a country boy from the nineteenth way, only a period behind. Talk turns at once to the First Law of Thek, which bars divulging scientific or technical knowledge. Hunter uses that rule to stage a comic clash between curiosity, custom, and the future's regulated life.
32126-freudian-slip:
Franklin Abel's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in May 1952, opens on the day the Earth vanished. Herman Raye, a tall, serious, sensitive young man with an outsize jaw and red-brown hair, is standing in a mountain stream in upstate New York, fishing for trout. It is the last day of his vacation, sunny and still, with trout biting. Herman wears heavy black-rimmed spectacles because his patients expect it. His reading runs to books on personality, behaviour disorders, and self-esteem.

In his off hours, Herman also likes baseball, beer, and bebop. The story's question, posed in its tagline, is whether things are exactly what they seem, and whether life is real and earnest. When the Earth vanishes beneath a man on holiday, that question stops being abstract. Readers get a witty, unsettling tale about perception, profession, and reality itself.
32400-paper-and-printing-recipes-a-handy:
J. Sawtelle Ford's Paper and Printing Recipes, entered for copyright in 1883 in Chicago, offers nearly two hundred practical recipes for stationers, printers, binders, and kindred trades. The recipes, gathered from many sources and endorsed by leading workmen in the United States and Europe, cover problems that arise in every day's work. Writing inks lead the index, with recipes for white, purple, cardinal, portable, and indelible inks, and for removing ink from paper.

Printing inks follow, with advice on keeping coloured inks from hardening or skinning, preserving them, brightening common qualities, and making dryers. Invisible writing, copying ink without press or water, and hektograph ink also appear. The book gives a clear, hands-on picture of the print shop and stationery trade in the late nineteenth century.
32522-mr-spaceship:
Philip K. Dick's tale, printed in Imagination in January 1953, imagines a human brain-controlled spacecraft, promising mechanical perfection with an unforeseen result: a strange entity called Mr. Spaceship. Kramer and Gross face a living minefield in war, where board plates show pseudopodia, living shapes no mechanical system can beat, simple or intricate. The Johnson Control must be scrapped, and war sits at stalemate, with neither side able to break through.

Kramer argues that a living thing still acts from necessity, like inanimate material, but with subtler, more complex cause and effect. A brain in a ship, Dick suggests, may solve the minefield problem while raising a stranger one: what the ship itself wants. The story pairs wartime engineering with early Dick themes of mind, machine, and identity, in a compact, unsettling form.
32563-the-lost-warship:
Robert Moore Williams's The Lost Warship, printed in Amazing Stories in January 1943, opens in a lifeboat on a glassy, motionless sea. Craig rigs a piece of sail for shade and rations water at a quarter cup a day. He faces Margy Sharp, who begs for a whole cup. She argues that the two of them, tough where the others are not, could get along together.

No wind has blown for three days, and the survivors drift with no ship in sight. Williams builds the story from thirst, suspicion, and a strange blast that changed the fate of the warship Idaho, as Craig weighs who will live when rescue seems far away.
32615-the-hell-ship:
Ray Palmer's The Hell Ship, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in March 1952, opens at White Sands Space Port. There the liner Prescott settles into its blast pit from the Jupiter run. No hatch opens and no person leaves, while armed Company men board a ship whose pilot looks massive, black-furred, and inhuman.

Gene O'Neil, a newspaperman for the Galactic Press Service, watches from outside the electrified wire. His editor wants him inside White Sands, though earlier men who tried have vanished, and Palmer builds dread from secrecy, rumor, and a crew no outsider has ever met.
33605-the-girl-aviators-and-the-phantom-:
Margaret Burnham follows Peggy Prescott and her brother Roy, a seventeen-year-old builder of flying machines, in this girls' aviation adventure. Peggy rushes down the garden path waving a newspaper that promises ambitious young aviators their chance, and Roy, hammer in hand in his workshop shed, shares her excitement. The siblings are determined to make their mark in the air.

The story's phantom airship gives their flying a mystery to chase, as the young aviators test machines, face rivals, and learn the discipline of early flight. Burnham writes briskly for young readers, mixing family warmth with the thrill of a new technology. The book captures an era when aviation still belonged to daring amateurs working in backyard sheds.
35531-countess-erika-s-apprenticeship:
Countess Erika's Apprenticeship is a German novel in English dress, issued in Philadelphia in the line of popular translations from the German made by Wister. The hosted copy opens with a long list of those translations: tales by Marlitt, Werner, Schubin, and others, bound in cloth for the American market. The novel itself dates from 1891 in the catalog.

German domestic novels of this school follow a young woman of rank as she learns the world. Erika's apprenticeship is in life rather than in trade: love, duty, and pride test her before she finds her place. Wister's renderings were loved for their smooth, warm English. Readers who enjoy Marlitt and her kin will find the same gentle, earnest world here.
35602-the-romantic-scottish-ballads-thei:
Robert Chambers wrote The Romantic Scottish Ballads: Their Epoch and Authorship, printed in 1849. Chambers opens by naming the books that made old Scottish song known, from Percy's Reliques of 1765 to Scott's Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border in 1802. He also cites Herd's Scottish Songs and Jamieson's Popular Ballads and Songs.

The question at the heart of the book is when the great ballads were made, and by whom. Chambers tests the claim that they came down by word of mouth from remote times. Students of song and folklore get a careful, early study of how a national store of tales in verse was built, printed, and argued over.
36007-ethel-morton-and-the-christmas-shi:
Mabell Smith wrote Ethel Morton and the Christmas Ship, a girls' book published at Chicago and New York by Donohue and Company. Ethel and her friends in the United Service Club plan a Christmas ship of gifts. Chapters cover financial plans, foraging by Roger, a search in the Smith attic, and goods for a traveller's kit. A Red Cross nurse sets sail, and the club puts on a show.

Later chapters show the girls sewing shirts for soldiers, weaving, stencilling, and cooking, until the Christmas ship sails at last. The story belongs to the First World War years, when American girls were urged to sew and save for soldiers and war orphans abroad.
3734-tom-swift-in-the-caves-of-ice-or-th:
Victor Appleton sends young inventor Tom Swift to the frozen north in this boys' adventure tale. Tom, helped by Ned and the faithful Mr Damon, builds and flies an airship after a map points to a valley of gold beyond the ice. Rival Andy Foger shadows them in his own triplane, and the race turns on storms, hail, musk oxen, and a rival claim jumped in the snow.

The middle chapters stage a wreck, a theft in the night, and a fight with native attackers, before the party reaches the caves of ice itself. Appleton writes at full tilt, with a new peril on nearly every page and a joke from Mr Damon to break the tension. Young readers who like machines, maps, and cold weather daring will find this one of the liveliest Tom Swift trips.
37386-cultus-arborum-a-descriptive-accou:
An unnamed scholar compiled this account of sacred tree worship, privately printed in 1890. The volume belongs to a series on symbol worship that included works on phallism and serpent worship. Its closely printed pages gather legends, customs, and rites from East and West.

The first chapter asks why men worship trees at all. The tree of life, the sacred fig, and the banyan carry the argument. India stands out as the great land of tree worship. Later chapters tour Persia, the Bible's holy trees, and the groves of the classics. Votive offerings hang in the branches throughout. A bibliography of nearly five hundred works closes the book, split between direct studies and books that touch the theme. The series served Victorian students of old faiths.
37982-the-golden-link-of-friendship:
Golden Link of Friendship is a small gift book of quotations, in a series of booklets. A line at its front calls friendship a link to bind when circumstances part. The booklet is split by themes, the first called Birth of Friendship. Short extracts from named authors fill each page. Cicero opens the set with a saying on how nature loves nothing solitary.

Addison follows with lines on great souls turning to each other. Emerson's saying that the only way to have a friend is to be one stands in the set. Jeremy Taylor sorts friendships into kinds, made by nature, contract, interest, or souls. Colton compares firm friendship to iron joined by fierce flame. Later pages in the copy argue that friendship born of God cannot lessen with time.
38723-a-prairie-courtship:
Harold Bindloss's prairie novel, copyrighted in 1910 by Stokes in New York and published in England as Alison's Adventure, opens on an emigrant train at dusk. Alison Leigh stands on the platform of a lurching car as the train runs through the last pine forest north of the Great Lakes toward Manitoba. It is early Canadian spring, with fangs of ice still in the river pools.

Alison, who must earn her living, shrinks from the stove-heated car and takes the bitter wind outside instead. The contents promise Maverick Thorne, the Farquhar homestead, a mortgage deed, and a bout of hail. Later chapters bring Corporal Slaney's defeat, Lucy going to the rescue, an open confession, and the reckoning.
39291-boy-labour-and-apprenticeship:
Reginald A Bray wrote this study of boy labour, printed by Constable of London in a second impression in 1912. Bray had written The Town Child. Press praise fills the front: the Times calls the problem acute in London and now felt in country towns. The Daily News urges the book on every student of social problems.

Chapters open with the essentials of apprenticeship, then trace the old system through the gilds, the Statute of Apprentices, and the industrial revolution. Later parts weigh what the state, charity, the home, and the workshop each owe the boy. Bray argues for training that fits a lad for skilled work, not blind alley jobs that waste his youth. The book is a reformer's brief, packed with counsel.
40059-wanderfoot-the-dream-ship:
Wanderfoot is a novel by Cynthia Stockley, printed at New York by Putnam's Sons in 1913. In England the book came out under the title The Dream Ship. Stockley also wrote Poppy and The Claw. The book is inscribed to her daughter Dorothy. It is in three parts, named for their settings: America, Jersey and France. A short poem about wandering fronts the tale.

The first part opens at sea. The Bavaric has been four fine September days out, and Westenra feels the grey pain that always haunts him after leaving Ireland. The voice of the Atlantic sings a dirge in his ears. Now none but the dead are left to him in the land of his birth. The novel follows an exile's wandering through three lands in search of peace.
40648-on-the-lightship:
On the Lightship is a set of tales by Herman Knickerbocker Viele, printed in New York by Duffield and Company in 1909. Thomas A Janvier wrote the opening. Viele had written The Inn of the Silver Moon, Myra of the Pines, and Heartbreak Hill.

The list holds The Story of Ignatius, the Almoner, The Dead Man Chest, and The Carhart Mystery. The Monstrosity, The Priestess of Amen Ra, and The Girl from Mercury follow. The Unexpected Letter, The Money Meter, The Guest of Honor, and The Man Without a Pension close the set. The first tale opens at the Butler Penfields garden party, where the results touch Miss Mabel Dunbar most. Mabel sells tea that all buy, since her grandmother had lived on Washington Square. Tale fans get society, mystery, and the strange in one volume.
41052-the-hallowell-partnership:
The Hallowell Partnership is a novel by Katharine Holland Brown, published in New York by Scribner in 1912. Brown had earlier written Philippa at Halcyon and The Messenger. The story first appeared in The Youth's Companion, whose courtesy the author acknowledges.

The frontispiece shows Marian, the heroine, lying by the fire teasing her cat Empress and fretting the endless hours away. Other illustrations show a quaint group on a river bank and Marian kneeling by a chair, clasping cold hands. The first chapter is titled When Slow-Coach Got His Start. A commodore and a Captain Lathrop appear in the plate captions, hinting at the book's older generation. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
41510-the-psychology-of-salesmanship:
The Psychology of Salesmanship is a business book by William Walker Atkinson, printed in London and in Massachusetts in 1912. Ten chapters make it up. They run from Psychology in Business through The Mind of the Salesman and The Mind of the Buyer. Then come The Pre-Approach, The Psychology of Purchase, The Approach, The Demonstration and The Closing.

Atkinson opens by noting a change in the business world. A few years before, he says, the word psychology in business drew a shrug and a raised eyebrow. Now they have learned that psychology means the science of the mind. They have seen that it plays a great part in business, and that its ground rules are worth their study. The book then works through the sale as a meeting of two minds.
45273-the-cabots-and-the-discovery-of-am:
The Cabots and the Discovery of America, by Elizabeth Hodges with pictures by Loxton, adds a brief description and history of Brandon Hill in Bristol, site of the Cabot Memorial Tower. Hodges opens with Bristol's famed church of Mary Redcliffe and the merchant William Canynge, who helped rebuild it. Against that remembered citizen she sets a forgotten one.

Canynge's work, she argues, was a drop in the ocean beside that of John Cabot, the merchant-pilot who found a continent and secured it for the English-speaking race. Yet Bristol, slow to honor merit from outside her borders, neglected the alien Cabot. His son Sebastian, claiming birth in Bristol, left tangled accounts that still stir dispute. Hodges writes local pride into a plain plea for the Cabots' due.
4608-tom-swift-in-captivity-or-a-daring-:
Victor Appleton opens Tom Swift in Captivity with Tom closing a book of adventures, yawning, and talking with his chum Ned Newton. A strange request from a circus man soon sends Tom off, with a warning to look out for a rival, alarming news, fire on board, and a narrow escape. Chapters follow a wild horse stampede, a living rope, a native battle, a desertion, and arrival in giant land, with a palace, a king, and a rival circus man.

Held captive, Tom uses a mysterious box, weak giants, a lone captive, a royal conspiracy, and twin giants to work toward freedom. The airship flight and Tom's giant close the tale. Readers get a lively boys' adventure of travel, giants, and invention, with humour and danger in equal measure, and with Tom's cool head turning a circus quest into a daring escape.
46540-elsie-s-winter-trip:
Elsie's Winter Trip, by Martha Finley, is a volume in the Elsie series. Dodd, Mead printed it in New York in 1902, the first edition coming that October. Finley had written Elsie Dinsmore, Elsie's Girlhood, and Mildred Keith before it.

A frontispiece shows Elsie's cabin, the trip of the title made visible. The tale opens on the first night in a new home. Chester asks his wife Lu for an early breakfast the next morning. The carriage is set for eight, the coachman Jack to drive him into town on business. Business, Chester owns, should have been seen to long before. Lu will rise and pour his coffee herself, saucy about it. He protests that she need not lose her rest for him. The parting that follows sets the household's tone of duty.
46696-a-new-system-of-horsemanship:
A New System of Horsemanship is a French work on the art of the horse. Bourgelat wrote it, and Richard Berenger put it in English. The book came out in London in the year 1754. Its first words say the art is old and loved in all ages.

The great have prized and used the art in each age, he holds. Yet its true worth lies in the real gains it brings the rider. The art has two parts, the plain of use and the fine of show. The fine part may be left aside with no loss to most men. No man who mounts a horse should lack the plain part, he says. Its use is to guide the horse and win his swift yield to the rein. A verse by Pope on the craft of verse heads the French work.
46775-tea-drinking-in-18th-century-ameri:
Tea Drinking in Eighteenth-Century America is a museum study by Rodris Roth. It appeared as paper fourteen in the Contributions from the Museum of History and Technology. Taking tea at home was an established social custom in colonial America, Roth writes. It had a recognized code of manners and its own furnishings. Pride was taken in a correct and fashionable tea table. Its equipage ran well beyond teapot, cups, and saucers.

The mistress of the house usually made and poured the tea. Guests had to handle cup and saucer neatly and supply conversation. Expense and time limited the tea party to the upper classes. The affair therefore worked as a status symbol. Roth compares it to the cocktail party of the twentieth century. An English family at tea, painted about 1720, illustrates the paper.
48241-an-american-religious-movement-a-b:
Winfred Ernest Garrison wrote An American Religious Movement, a brief history of the Disciples of Christ, printed in Saint Louis in 1945. Garrison asks who the Disciples are, where their churches began, and how they grew into a major American group. The tale starts early in the nineteenth century.

Two streams of reform joined, both seeking to cut past creeds to the plain teaching of the early church. The coming of the Campbells, years with the Baptists, and a break to independence fill the middle chapters. Later parts cover growth, strain, and a slow maturing down to 1945. The book is a clear, short map of one home-grown movement of faith.
48278-rites-and-ritual-a-plea-for-aposto: Rites and Ritual: A Plea for Apostolic Doctrine and Worship is a theological treatise by Philip Freeman, vicar of Thorverton in Devon and archdeacon and canon of Exeter. Freeman had already written The Principles of Divine Service. John Murray printed the book at London in 1866, in a fourth edition revised. An appendix contains the opinions of Henry, Lord Bishop of Exeter, on certain points of doctrine. The plea defends ceremonial worship and apostolic teaching within the Church of England, in the heat of the ritual controversies.
4913-chess-and-checkers-the-way-to-maste:
Edward Lasker's manual teaches chess and checkers together, moving from rules to mastery in clear stages. The chess half covers special terms, move symbols, and laws. Then come elementary tactics and fundamental endings. It weighs the value of the pieces and sets out general plans for king's pawn and queen's pawn openings and the middle game.

Illustrative games follow, including Lasker against Capablanca at New York in 1915 and against Showalter at Lexington in 1917, with problems for practice. The checkers half mirrors the plan, from rules to five fundamental positions. Players who want to improve get a structured course, not just a set of games.
50794-the-haunted-ship:
Kate Tucker wrote a children's tale printed at New York in 1929, with pictures by Ethel Taylor. Ann could feel the dory rise and plunge, the frontispiece says. Jo Bailey and three Seymours opens the chapters, then the wrecked schooner and how the boat came ashore. In the good greenwood and on the wreck follow.

Going lobstering, painting the deer, and a man with a lantern fill the middle. A day of mysteries, the fire in the woods, and through the porthole raise the stakes. The figurehead's secret and a reason for everything close the book. Jo Bailey flipped the reins over the lumbering nag, eager to see what the Seymours would be like. They were coming from Boston to spend the summer at the Bailey house.
51434-an-elephant-for-the-prinkip:
An Elephant for the Prinkip is a science fiction tale by L J Stecher, first printed in Galaxy Magazine in August 1960. Dick Francis drew its illustrations. Its blurb warns that a Delta class freighter can carry anything, maybe more than its skipper can bear. The narrator is a trader with a load of Gasha root. The root will spoil if it stays on the ground. At Helmholtz Spaceport he spots a Delta freighter he does not know. It sits under the gantry, not yet signed for a cargo.

The ship is the Delta Crucis, a tramp. Her skipper is a lean man with pale spacer's eyes. The two size each other up over a glass of rhial in the port bar. The trader sounds him out on a rough cargo job. The tale turns on what such a ship can be made to swallow, and at what price.
51741-round-and-round-trip:
Round-and-Round Trip, a story by H B Fyfe, comes from the December 1960 issue of Galaxy Magazine. It begins at a spaceport of St Andrew the Fifth. Robert L Winstead, a tired, clerkish traveler in a maroon suit, joins the line at the Interstellar Travel Agency counter. He wears one blue sock and one green. Most passengers are staying; Winstead carries an ultimate destination ticket. The brisk young clerk stamps his papers, stops in puzzlement at the destination card, and asks whether he has mixed his ticket up with someone else's.

The headnote gives the game away. All the man wanted was to go from here to there, but the whole Milky Way had been turned into a squirrel cage. Fyfe builds the tale on the comedy of interstellar timetables and connections that never connect.
53063-the-netherworld-of-mendip:
The Netherworld of Mendip is a book of cave exploration by Ernest Baker and Herbert Balch. It was issued in 1907 from Clifton and London. Its subtitle promises explorations in the great caverns. Somerset, Yorkshire, and Derbyshire are its chief ground. The contents list runs from the Mendip district to single caves. A map of swallets and cave mouths opens the text.

Chapters treat the Cheddar group and the age of the caves. Cave exploring as a sport gets its own chapter. Wookey Hole and Swildon's Hole are explored in detail. Five caverns at Cheddar follow, then Burrington. A coral cave and Lamb's Lair come next. Welsh and Irish caves widen the range at the end. Photos show pottery, coins, and bones from Wookey. The book made potholing known as a sport.
53712-the-boy-inventors-flying-ship:
Richard Bonner wrote The Boy Inventors’ Flying Ship, a tale of young makers and a craft that flies and floats. Hurst and Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred thirteen. Charles L Wrenn drew the pictures. Bonner had written other Boy Inventors tales of wireless and diving boats.

Jack Chadwick and his cousin Tom Jesson built the ship, named Wondership. Pontoons let her rest on water as well as fly. The boys plan a night test to dodge prying crowds. A Boston paper has dubbed their craft a night sky riddle. Chapters promise a stowaway, a mutiny, and a storm at sea. Castaways, a whale, and Amazon tribes wait past the wreck. Diamonds test the boys at the close.
54088-narrative-of-a-voyage-to-hudson-s-:
Lieutenant Edward Chappell of the Royal Navy wrote an account of a voyage to Hudson Bay in the ship Rosamond, printed at London in 1817. The full title says the book also treats the north east coast of America. It treats the tribes who lived in that far region too. A map of the Great Nelson River heads the book.

Chappell gives the book to Lord Viscount Palmerston, then Secretary of War. He thanks him and calls the book a mark of respect. The map shows portages, falls, and rapids from Lake Winnipeg to Gull Lake. Depths of each fall are marked in feet. The tale gives a plain sea officer's view of a cold and far coast.
54364-the-brighton-boys-in-the-submarine:
James R Driscoll wrote The Brighton Boys in the Submarine Treasure Ship, a boys’ sea tale. The John C Winston Company issued the book in Philadelphia in nineteen hundred twenty. Driscoll held a lieutenant’s rank in the late war. Ten Brighton Boys war tales had come before this one.

Jay Thacker and Dick Monaghan sail home on the great Leviathan. Two years of fleet war made ensigns of the school boys. A strange shape in the sea starts their new quest at once. The pair sign up for salvage work on a gold trail. A lost U-boat is found with goods still in her hold. The Jules Verne, a fine diving ship, joins the hunt in time. A trapped diving bell and a brave dog crowd the mid tale. The loot is won back, and Brighton cheers its boys home.
54501-two-dianas-in-somaliland-the-recor:
Two Dianas in Somaliland is the record of a shooting trip by Agnes Herbert, issued at London by John Lane in 1908. Twenty five pictures from photographs illustrate the book. Its dedication teases the leader of the opposition shoot. He is called soldier, shikari, and sometime misogynist in her address.

Herbert owns that the world is not panting for another tale of a shoot. Of the making of sporting books there is no end, she admits. Simply, she says, I want to write, and writes anyway. Her record tells of a big shoot engineered and carried through by two women. That fact sets the book apart in its sporting age. Lions, oryx, and desert camps fill a woman’s safari tale.
54533-the-cruise-of-the-dream-ship:
Cruise of the Dream Ship is a sailing voyage tale by Ralph Stock. Doubleday Page of Garden City issued the book in nineteen twenty two. Photographs illustrate it, with line drawings by Lynn Bogue Hunt inside. Parts first ran under National Geographic auspices in nineteen twenty.

Stock gives the book to Peter and Steve on the dedication page. Chapters open on the dream and the means to realize such dreams. Preparation and personnel follow, then Vigo off the coast of Spain comes. The Canary Islands, the Atlantic start, and the British West Indies follow. Through the Panama Canal to the Galapagos and Marquesas the ship sails. Paumotu atolls and Papeete, Tahiti, close the listed ports of call.
54577-a-wedding-trip:
Emilia Pardo Bazan wrote A Wedding Trip, a Spanish novel translated by Mary Serrano and published at New York in 1891 by the Cassell Publishing Company. Serrano had translated the journal of Marie Bashkirtseff. The novel opens at the railway station at Leon, where a wedding party gathers. At a glance the wedding is not a fashionable one. The bride and groom might mix in select society, but most of the guests belong to the middle class that merges into the mass of the people.

The two escorts differ sharply in social condition, and that gap drives the story of the marriage trip that follows. Pardo Bazan was Spain's leading novelist of her generation, noted for exact social observation.
54962-retail-shoe-salesmanship: Retail Shoe Salesmanship is a training course book for men who sell shoes in shops. The Retail Shoe Salesmen's Institute ran the course as a study plan for the trade. Long lists of founders and backers fill the front pages. They name shoe firms and makers from Boston, St Louis, Brooklyn and many other towns. The book rests on trade support and aims to school shop staff in their craft.
55858-the-girl-scouts-canoe-trip:
Edith Lavell wrote a Girl Scouts novel in 1922, one of a series that includes the girls at school and at camp. Five new canoes lie upturned on the shore of Silver Creek, bright with paint and varnish. An old boatman at a rustic boathouse watches and thinks of his own youth. The girls are amateur canoeists setting off on a trip.

Chapters cover the first camp, an accident, and an adventure on an island. A search, prisoners, a storm, and a pursuit raise the stakes. A house party, a tennis tournament, and a canoe meet fill the late chapters. Marjorie paddles hard to take second place in the meet.
55993-the-diamond-ship:
The Diamond Ship is a sea tale by Max Pemberton, out in nineteen twelve. The book is writ with thanks to a late head of his old school, his past guide. Past twenty parts fill it, each with a note of whose voice tells it. A news man opens the tale, then a wife tells of her brothers come back to a hall.

A doctor then takes up his own tale, of a man with three fingers, a call from a wife, and his yacht. Parts sail to Africa, to far isles, and to a cave in the hills. A strong room of the sea, a light stack, and a red sky flare mark the late parts. The tale turns on a strange ship and the men who defy its crew.
56552-patty-s-pleasure-trip:
Carolyn Wells wrote a girls novel about Patty and a trip to Europe, printed in New York in 1909. Wells also wrote the Marjorie books and the Two Little Women books. The tale opens at the Grange, where Patty sits deep in a book while friends talk of hats and ribbons. A summons home soon changes her plans.

A pleasure trip is offered, and a farewell party sends Patty off. Days in Paris come first, then Rome with its old glory, tea, and new friends. Florence and Venice follow, with pigeons, verse, and one sharp adventure. The last chapter turns homeward. Light talk, clothes, sights, and friendship carry the book for young readers.
57409-the-book-of-friendship-a-little-ma:
Reginald Wright Kauffman wrote The Book of Friendship, a little manual of comradeship, printed at Philadelphia with rights held in 1909. A line of Emerson fronts it: services are eaten like apples and forgotten, but love a man and he feels you and delights in you all the time. So, if I live or die to serve my friend, a verse adds, tis for my love.

Kauffman gathers the wisdom of the poets and sages on what a friend is and does. The book is small, gilt, and made to give away, in the Altemus gift-book manner. Give me the avowed, erect, manly foe stands among its mottoes. Readers get a warm pocket companion on the oldest bond.
57440-a-soldier-s-experience-in-southern:
A Soldier's Experience in Southern Prisons, by Prutsman, a lieutenant in the Seventh Regiment of Wisconsin Volunteers, was published at New York in 1901. Its subtitle promises a graphic description of the author's time in various southern prisons. Chapter one covers the events before his capture, his last day of freedom, and the taking of his picket line. He loses a valuable pair of boots on the road through Warrenton and Culpepper.

Chapter two brings him to Libby Prison, where he loses his money and is greeted as fresh fish by older prisoners. Later pages tell of the smallpox ward, escape plans, and a tunnel over a powder mine. Cries of bread, hopes of exchange, and moves to Danville and Macon fill the contents. Such memoirs kept the prison story of the Civil War before the public. Prutsman writes as a common soldier who endured it.
57837-the-gift-of-friendship:
Alfred Hyatt chose and edited The Gift of Friendship, a small book printed in London and Edinburgh in 1910. Water-color pictures by Preston Macgoun decorate it. The contents run from Emerson on friendship to Thoreau, Carlyle, Goldsmith, Johnson, Steele, and Addison on the same theme.

Later pages add Bacon, Montaigne, and Aristotle, plus a letter on ideal friendship. Each writer treats a side of the bond: how friends are won, what they give, and how to choose them well. Hyatt shaped the set as a gift book, short enough to give and rich enough to keep. It gathers four centuries of thought on one warm subject in a few sittings.
57941-engineer-port-repair-ship:
Engineer Port Repair Ship is War Department Technical Manual TM 5-362, issued at Washington in October 1944 and marked restricted. It is the official guide for the Army engineer crews who manned special ships fitted to repair damaged ports in wartime. An order signed for the Secretary of War by Chief of Staff Marshall sent it to armies, corps, and the engineer units that crewed the ships.

Sections cover the mission and how the ships relate to other units, the crew jobs and duties, and full lists of ship gear and supplies. Later parts set out crew training, underway drills, and the work of clearing and fixing a wrecked harbor. It preserves the paper side of a little known wartime service.
59645-our-base-ball-club-and-how-it-won-:
Noah Brooks wrote Our Base Ball Club and How It Won the Championship, published in New York in 1884, with an introduction by Spalding of the Chicago base ball club. Brooks had written The Fairport Nine. Spalding opens by marveling that, given the game's strong hold on the people, more writers had not used it as a frame for story.

Brooks does just that, building a novel on a club's run to a championship. A front picture shows a judge's daughter being called to breakfast, a hint of the home life woven round the team. The book is an early baseball novel, written when the pro game was young, and it treats players as heroes for boys to follow.
60468-devil-worship:
Devil Worship presents the sacred books and traditions of the Yezidiz, in a study by Isya Joseph published at Boston in 1919. Joseph wrote it for a series on world worships. He thanks teachers at Union, Columbia, and Harvard in the dedication.

An opening part tells how the Arabic manuscript came to him at Mosul. A friend gave it as a keepsake before Joseph left the city. The book then gives the text in English, with parts on Al-Jilwah and other lore. Readers get a rare early account, in English, of a faith long closed and often misjudged by outsiders.
61363-the-universal-kinship:
The Universal Kinship is a book on the kin of man and beast by Moore, a teacher of beast lore at a high school of Chicago. A verse at its head gives its creed: a holy kin I would not lose binds me to all that breathes. It came out at Chicago in the first years of the last age.

Its gift word makes it out to his mum and dad, who did so much for him in the long years past and gone. Its parts run in three great heads. First the kin of the frame: man an beast, man a back bone kind, man a milk kind, man a first of his tribe. Then the kin of the mind, and last the kin of the heart and its dues.
61679-the-girl-scouts-motor-trip:
Edith Lavell wrote this volume of her Girl Scouts series, copyrighted in 1924. Marjorie Wilkinson and her troop had already been to Miss Allen's school, to camp, and on a canoe trip. The frontispiece shows the troop around a campfire, smelling bacon and coffee.

The tale opens at Turner College after a hockey match. Marjorie's sophomores have beaten the juniors, and Lily Andrews crows over her captain. Florence Evans, an old Pansy Troop patrol member now a freshman, comes for the news. A challenge arrives to set the motor trip going. Lavell writes brisk, wholesome adventure for girls, with scouting woven through school and road alike.
62792-the-boy-scouts-and-the-army-airshi:
Howard Payson, writing as a lieutenant, told of The Boy Scouts and the Army Airship. The Burt company issued it in New York, under a nineteen eleven copyright. A front plate shows a flier roaring directly above the boys' heads. Payson had written of the Eagle Patrol and the Panama Canal scouts before.

Sea Scouts at Play opens the tale on the water. The spearing of a sturgeon and the return of Jack Curtiss follow. Paul Perkins and his motor scooter bring the machine age in. Two mysterious men and a secret passage thicken the plot. Captain Hudgins's bees swarm at the crisis. An army airship crowns the boys' adventures in the new sky.
63041-morgue-ship:
Morgue Ship is a science fiction tale by Ray Bradbury of the dead in space. The story ran in Planet Stories for Summer nineteen forty four. Sam Burnett works the morgue ship Constellation on his last trip out. Three more shelves to fill, and he will be among the living again.

Metal claws grope into space and pluck dead warriors from the void. Pallid bodies lie on cold clear tables while machines hum around them. Shelves rise and fall, numbered in scarlet, to keep the fallen safe. Ten years of this run from Earth to nowhere has worn Burnett down. A red haze clouds his mind as another dead man comes aboard.
63160-forest-glen-or-the-mohawk-s-friend:
Forest Glen, or The Mohawk's Friendship is a boys' novel by Elijah Kellogg. Lee and Shepard of Boston published it in 1877. Kellogg wrote the Elm Island Stories and the Pleasant Cove series too. A bear fight serves as the frontispiece. His preface frames the tale against Pennsylvania's frontier years. Many races and sects then shared that soil with little in common.

An Indian war held that mixed people together by fear. The preface pictures a Quaker tilling his land in peace. His neighbour sleeps with a rifle within reach. Men sat in church with weapons between their knees. Funeral processions went armed, and were often attacked. Kellogg promises useful lessons and incentives to manly effort. Frontier peril and a Mohawk's friendship carry the story.
63950-star-ship:
Poul Anderson wrote Star Ship, a science fiction tale printed in Planet Stories in the fall of nineteen hundred fifty. A Terran star ship hangs empty in orbit about Khazak. Her whole crew went down in a life boat to scout that Iron Age world. The life boat cracked up on landing.

Dougald Anson sails home to Krakenau harbor in rain and dark. No torch, song, or new street light greets his boat. The rich port should ring with feast night noise, he thinks. A dead town waits where a loud one stood days before. Anson has fought pirates and kings on these coasts for years. He dries off, dons ring mail, and steps ashore with care. Castaway spacemen and a hushed town start Anderson’s tale of two worlds.
66349-the-cosmic-courtship:
Julian Hawthorne wrote The Cosmic Courtship, a novel of the future that opens on June 22 in the year 2001. Miriam Mayne turns twenty-one that day, and the world has learned to fly.

Miriam's father Terence, a billionaire contractor, heads downtown to business. She dresses for travel in a dove-colored tunic and trousers cut to the knee. Winged sandals, a winged cap, and a knobbed belt complete her flying gear. Personal flight is still a novelty, though its principle is known. She steps from her balcony, poised above the court, and rises into a glorious morning. Hawthorne builds romance on the wonders of a new century.
6678-nonsenseorship:
G. G. Putnam gathers writers like Heywood Broun, Dorothy Parker, Ben Hecht, Alexander Woollcott, and the author of The Mirrors of Washington to mock bans on books and drink. The opening joke sets the tone: Haig and Haig costs twelve dollars a quart, while a booklegger can find Jurgen for fifteen, an economic case for nonsenseorship. Pictures by Ralph Barton add bite.

Essays on prohibitions, inhibitions, and illegalities follow, with wit aimed at censors of the 1920s. The tone is gay, sharp, and free, not solemn. Nonsenseorship is a lively period protest, fun for readers who like literary mischief and free-speech history.
67355-iola-us-an-anthology-of-friendship:
Edward Carpenter gathers what the ages wrote on friendship in an anthology issued at London in 1906. Swan Sonnenschein published this second, enlarged edition. The title names Iolaus, friend of Hercules.

Plutarch's words front the book. Lovers, he says, still swear fidelity at the tomb of Iolaus. Chapter one treats friendship customs in the pagan and early world. Blood tasting and name exchange mark those rites. Greek life and thought take the major part, since Greek sources run rich. Greek and Roman poetry of friendship follows. Early Christian and medieval times come next. The Renaissance and modern times close the survey, with additions dated 1906. Carpenter, the socialist poet of fellowship, built the book as a brief for comrade love across history.
67786-santa-s-sampler-a-collection-of-ov:
Santas Sampler is a fund raising cook book of party snacks. Women of a Saint Louis alumnae group gave the recipes for the book. Sale funds go to a sorority fund and a school for children. The book bears the year nineteen seventy six on its front art.

More than one hundred recipes fill five short parts in the book. Hot dips and spreads lead, then hot and cold small bites in turn. A last part gives gifts a cook can make at home for the feast. Names of the cooks who gave each dish are kept with the recipes. One dip mixes canned tomatoes and soft cheese to serve with corn chips.
68159-good-citizenship:
Good Citizenship is a pair of essays by Grover Cleveland, published in Philadelphia by the Henry Altemus Company in 1908. Cleveland, twice president of the United States, writes here as a private moralist. The contents join the title essay with a second on patriotism and holiday observance.

He opens by fearing his subject is too familiar to interest anyone. Americans, he argues, hold a self satisfied notion of citizenship. They profess the creed and avoid palpable unpatriotic sins, and think that enough. Cleveland insists that good citizenship demands active and affirmative participation. He resents the preachers who badger, yet takes their side in substance. The little book is a former president's sermon on duty, delivered in the plain style of his veto messages.
68493-promoting-good-citizenship:
Promoting Good Citizenship is a pair of essays by James Bryce. Houghton Mifflin issued it in the Riverside Essays series. The price was thirty-five cents, postpaid. The essays began as lectures on the Dodge Foundation at Yale. Yale University Press first printed them as a book. Their first title was The Hindrances to Good Citizenship. This school edition shortens that name.

The first essay is called Indolence. It opens with a tale of Doctor Johnson and his dictionary. Asked about a blunder, Johnson blamed sheer ignorance. Bryce turns that joke toward civic sloth. Men let chances to learn and act slip by, he says. Laziness, fear of effort, and trust in luck all hinder. The second essay shows how to beat those hindrances. Bryce wrote as a friend and student of America.
68987-on-the-manner-of-negotiating-with-:
Callieres, a French envoy who helped make the peace at Ryswick and sat in the French Academy, wrote On the Manner of Negotiating with Princes, first printed at Paris in 1716. Whyte Englished this text, printed at Boston and New York in 1919. The book treats the uses of statecraft and the choice of envoys.

A long first note in this edition ties the old rules to the Great War just past. It faults the love of secret deals and asks if light on great powers can curb war. Envoys get plain laws on the traits a good agent needs. Readers get a classic guide that still reads fresh.
69916-the-last-space-ship:
The Last Space Ship is a science fiction novel by Murray Leinster, here in a 1949 Galaxy novel reprint at thirty five cents. It is Galaxy novel number twenty five. Copyright stands in Leinster's real name, Will Jenkins, on the page.

Part one, The Disciplinary Circuit, runs from Victim of Tyrants to Haven at Last. Rays of destruction and outcasts of space fill its middle chapters. Part two, The Manless Worlds, turns to empires in the making. Deadly beams, a contact in the void, and a man made meteor build the close. Readers get a full Leinster novel of rebels against a galactic tyranny, in cheap paper dress.
70166-the-katcina-altars-in-hopi-worship:
The Katcina Altars in Hopi Worship is a study by Fewkes, chief of the national house for the lore of the first peoples of America. It was drawn from a state report of the mid nineteen twenties and put out by the state print house at Washington. Three plates show the shrines it treats.

A key to the plates names each part of the shrines in turn. A sun spirit, a spray tool, corn mounds and ears, a gourd, and a plant stick stand in the list. Signs for storm flash, a bowl of rite stuff, prayer sticks, a war god, and prayer meal are named as well. The study tells how the Hopi set and use these altars in their rites.
7019-for-auld-lang-syne-a-book-of-friend:
Ray Woodward selects a book of friendship for Auld Lang Syne, dedicating it with affection to his father Fred Woodward. The introduction holds friendship essentially the same bond whether it joins persons of intellect and refined taste or those with little sense of their mission or duty. Its forms may differ wholly, yet the two friendships share points in common, drawing friends close in a bond praised through the ages.

No single philosopher's abstract theory can satisfy a reader on friendship's varied forms, Woodward argues. It proves interesting and profitable to note what various writers have said of this world wide force under past and present conditions. The book gathers those voices into a gift volume on an old and lasting tie.
70295-uncle-wiggily-s-airship:
Uncle Wiggily's Airship is a bedtime story book by Howard Garis. Burt Company of New York put the book out in the year 1915. Louis Wisa drew the pictures for the old rabbit's air voyage. Garis had writ Sammie and Susie Littletail and the Wagtail books before. The Uncle Wiggily books sold at seventy-five cents each in cloth.

Eight coloured illustrations stand in each volume of that long line. Uncle Wiggily's Adventures heads the list of the rabbit's many books. Baby Bunty, Old Mother Hubbard, and the seashore fill other volumes. Buddy and Brighteyes Pigg, Bully and Bawly No-Tail, join the cast. Charlie and Arabella Chick and the Twisty-Tail pigs have their own books. Daddy series and Island Boys series fill the back list pages. The airship tale lifts the old gentleman rabbit into the sky.
70392-nobody-saw-the-ship:
Nobody Saw the Ship is a science fiction novelette by Murray Leinster. The story appeared in a magazine of 1950 that joined two older titles. A blurb calls it a powerful tale of a tiny scout ship from beyond the stars. One alien rides the ship, and its mission means death to all life on Earth.

The landing of the scout craft, fifteen feet across, passes wholly unseen. Its pilot seeks a hormone stuff that his people's science says must exist. His race cannot make the stuff, yet needs it in great bulk to live. The ray guns of his kind would destroy the prize, so stealth rules the search. The ship tests Neptune, a moon of Jupiter, and Mars in turn. Against the raider, the blurb promises, stand one frightened old man and his dog.
71692-toffee-takes-a-trip:
Charles Myers wrote this comic fantasy for Fantastic Adventures in July 1947. Marc Pillsworth decided he needed a vacation, the blurb explains at the front. But where Marc went, Toffee followed, with trouble in her wake, it promises of the tale.

Glumly, in sandy discomfort, Marc watched another wave trip and fall flat, the story opens. The sameness of the beach was getting him down on his holiday there. His stomach had burned vermillion while his back reached tomato soup, he reports, and Toffee, a lovely ghost of his own daydreams, is about to make the trip unforgettable.
72237-peck-s-bad-boy-in-an-airship:
George Peck, the Wisconsin humorist and former governor, sent his Bad Boy up in an airship in this tale, published in Chicago in 1908. Charles Lederer drew the pictures. A caption shows the boy inviting a victim to take that from your little Hennery.

Peck's Bad Boy and his Pa are sent to Europe to study airships, with an eye to using them in the United States Navy. Their adventures run from European capitals to South Africa, where the airship goes hunting wild animals. Peck writes broad dialect comedy around the newest wonder of the age. Readers get the Bad Boy at full altitude.
72612-uncle-wiggily-s-fishing-trip:
Howard Garis wrote this little picture book, Uncle Wiggily's Fishing Trip, pictured by Lang Campbell and issued at Newark and New York in 1919. Its full title promises the good luck he had with the clothes hook, how the Pip and Skee were stuck by the chestnut burrs, and the good time at the marshmallow roast. A library plate at the front begs the child, in rhyme, to bring the book back when read.

Uncle Wiggily is the bunny rabbit gentleman of Garis's famous newspaper stories, rheumatic, kind, and always in small adventures. The book lists its mates in the series: the auto sled, the snow man, the apple roast, and more. Garis wrote such books by the hundred. This one is a fishing trip for the youngest readers.
73748-white-house-gossip:
Edna M Colman wrote White House Gossip, from Andrew Johnson to Calvin Coolidge. Doubleday, Page and Company issued the book at Garden City in nineteen hundred twenty seven. Photographs of presidents and their wives crowd its bright plates. Eighteen parts, one per reign, divide the house’s long tale.

Mrs Calvin Coolidge fronts the book in its first fine plate. Andrew Johnson’s small first tailor shop shows his lowly start here. April of eighteen hundred sixty five found Washington in black crape. Lincoln’s death by night had stunned the grieving capital city. Grant, Hayes, Garfield, and Arthur take their turns in the tale. Cleveland’s two reigns and his bride’s gay gown earn full plates. McKinley, Roosevelt, Taft, and Wilson fill the next wide span. Harding laid in state closes the grave roll of house lore.
73829-elsie-s-scholarship:
Elsie Scholarship and Why She Surrendered It is a girls tale by Emma Leslie. Gall and Inglis of London and Edinburgh published the tract style story. A frontispiece shows a master congratulating both you scholarship girls in the scene. Contents open with candidates, the examination, and the master proposal in the plot.

A brave resolution follows, with Tom illness and Jack Bond entering the tale. Changes, a new home, a bicycle, and a memorable fight fill the middle chapters. Herbert Milner, enquiries, and earnest endeavours lead toward Tom scholarship at the end. Chapter one calls out Elsie Winn, Mary Nicholls, and Jane Holmes as candidates.
74436-tim-and-tip:
Tim and Tip, or The Adventures of a Boy and a Dog, is a boys' novel by James Otis, author of Toby Tyler. Harper and Brothers copyrighted it in 1883, and this is the large-type edition in Harper's Young People's Series. An illustration shows Tim bearing the marks of Captain Babbige's whip. The contents open with Tim's flight, then Sam the fat boy, and Tip's introduction to Mrs Simpson.

Tim's start in life and his life on board the Pride of the Wave carry the middle chapters. A notice preserved in the copy gives the boy's description as a runaway. Strayed: a boy from the home of the subscriber, about eleven years old, with short, light hair, a turned-up nose, and a face very much tanned. When last seen he wore a faded, worn suit of blue clothes, and he had the dog with him.
74700-my-toughest-trip:
Sergeant Reading, late of the Arctic patrols of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, tells in My Toughest Trip of the rescue that stayed with him: an Eskimo baby. Most Arctic trouble, he says, came from clashes between white traders and natives, or from quarrels among the tribes over women. In this case two men had stolen a girl from her lawful husband in another tribe.

The two men were sentenced to two years of chores at the post at Tree River, and Reading was detailed to sail her back to her husband. He loaded the sailboat with grub for six weeks and set out one bright June morning. Two weeks of contrary winds followed, then a storm that washed them ashore on an island. The boat lay stranded a quarter of a mile from the water, beyond one man's strength to move.
74763-lost-gip:
Lost Gip, a story by Hesba Stretton, was reprinted from a penny weekly called The Day of Rest. King published it at London in 1873, in its eleventh thousand, with six illustrations. Stretton had already won fame with Jessica's First Prayer and Little Meg. The contents begin with Gip's first breath and Gip's home.

Then Gip is lost in London, and lost in Jerusalem by turn. A new friend, Mrs Shafto, and a sad sight follow. Seeking the lost, an awakened conscience, and two mothers fill the middle chapters. Johnny's Sunday suit, a passing away, and found at last bring the tale toward its close. Stretton's stories of street children moved Victorian readers to tears and to charity. Gip is one of her waifs, lost in the great city under a smiting sun and dirty streets. The book joins a child's suffering to a call for mercy.
75995-pistol-marksmanship:
Pistol Marksmanship, Marine Corps Reference Publication 3-01B, is the Marine Corps source document for pistol training. Headquarters Marine Corps issued it at Washington on November 25, 2003, approved for public release with unlimited distribution. The foreword states the case: a Marine must deliver well-aimed shots to end a threat, without escalating violence or causing needless collateral damage. Good firearms are not enough; training must prepare Marines to fire accurately under the worst conditions.

The manual covers skill with the M9, the 9-millimetre service pistol, and its care and maintenance. A well-trained Marine, it says, is confident he can protect himself, do the mission, and protect his fellow Marines. The front matter invites readers to send suggested changes to the Doctrine Division at Quantico. The text uses the masculine gender for both men and women, as its notice states.
76976-the-art-of-courtship:
Clement Wood wrote The Art of Courtship, issued as Little Blue Book number 988 at Girard, Kansas, with a copyright of 1926. The little books, edited by Haldeman-Julius, sold for a few cents and put plain talk in every pocket. Wood opens by asking why one must woo, and where wooing began.

Chapters follow on whom to woo, with physical, mental, and social mates weighed, then how a man woos and how a woman woos. A last part treats conduct during the engagement and the proposal. Wood writes frankly for his day, with humor and a modern view of women as full persons. The booklet is a sample of the cheap, bold self-help of the 1920s.
77867-through-the-sun-in-an-airship:
Through the Sun in an Airship is a tale of wonder by John Mastin, printed at London by Griffin and Company. Mastin, a fellow of several learned bodies, had written The Stolen Planet and The Immortal Light. He gave this book to his old teacher, the artist Hubert von Herkomer, and dated his gift page at Totley Brook near Sheffield in June 1909.

The tale opens with the story of the Regina, a ship that gives up her secret chapter by chapter. Later heads promise a doomed planet, the story of a star, a Jovian bug, and a passage through fire and flame. Mastin mixes science, jest, and marvel in a voyage between two worlds.
78876-two-english-queens-and-philip:
Two English Queens and Philip is a history by Martin Hume, first published by Methuen of London in 1908. Hume edited the Calendars of Spanish State Papers, and the book draws on that archive. Its queens are Mary and Elizabeth of England. Its Philip is the king of Spain who married one and courted the other.

The chapters follow the Spanish match, Wyatt's rebellion, and Cardinal Pole. Persecution and the loss of Calais darken Mary's reign. Her death brings Elizabeth to the throne and a fresh offer from Philip. Peace at Cateau-Cambresis fails to settle the rivalry. Mary Stuart's claim, Spanish ambassadors, and plots fill the later chapters. Hume writes narrative history with a Spanish-side view of the evidence. The book remains a readable account of England's most dangerous marriage diplomacy.
79231-judge-ben-b-lindsey-on-the-child-t:
Judge Ben Lindsey on the Child, the Movie, and Censorship is a talk tract past that judge of the young folk court of a west town. Four sharp lines head it. One dares any man to show that a town or state with screen bans is one whit the best past free ones. One calls the film a true league of lands, that binds the world past the sight that all men are the same.

A front sketch tells he was made guard of that countys young folk in January of eighteen ninety-nine. Past that year he was made judge of that court and has been chose past ten times since.
