A fame book calls him the spur of the young court plan and a world known voice on young crime. The talk was given at a film meet in a lake town in February of nineteen twenty-six.
79439-the-slave-ship:
Mary Johnston wrote The Slave Ship, a historical novel published by Little, Brown of Boston in 1924. Johnston lists her earlier tales at the front: Silver Cross, 1492, and Croatan. Her narrator is David Scott, a young Scot of twenty-two. He fought for the Stuarts at Prestonpans, Falkirk, and Culloden.

After Culloden, Scott lies in irons in the Tolbooth at Edinburgh. Transport to Barbados or Virginia awaits him if hanging does not. He fashions a file from a clamped bit of iron off the wall. A week later, on a dark and stormy night, he squeezes through the window and drops into the lane. Johnston sends her Jacobite toward the sea, and toward the slave ship of the title.
79644-democracy-and-leadership:
Irving Babbitt wrote Democracy and Leadership, published at Boston and New York in 1924. The catalog title keeps only the second word of the name. Babbitt also wrote Rousseau and Romanticism and The New Laokoon, and he taught French and comparative literature at Harvard.

Babbitt opens with two hard sayings, one from Aristotle on private property and one on the need for a controlling power over will and appetite. His argument follows from them: a democracy still needs leaders formed by restraint and tradition. He distrusts both unchecked mass feeling and unchecked wealth. The book is a founding text of the New Humanism, Babbitt's case for discipline in public and private life.
8855-astral-worship:
J. H. Hill, a physician, opens Astral Worship with a demand for facts, quoting Boz. Then argues that much of religion, including Christian festivals, grew from worship of the sun and stars. Contents move from the geocentric system, earth, firmament, planets, constellations. Zodiac, through the sacred numbers seven and twelve and a twelve-thousand-year cycle, to the ancient triad, God Sol, ancient cosmogony, and the fall and redemption of man.

Incarnations of God Sol, the fable of the twelve labours. Anniversaries of solar worship follow: nativity, epiphany, Lent, passion week, resurrection and Easter, annunciation, ascension, assumption, the Lord's Supper, and even an autumnal crucifixion and Michaelmas. Hill's thesis, once popular in freethought circles, is now largely rejected by scholars, and readers should treat it as a period argument, not settled history. Even so, it is a vivid example of nineteenth-century mythic speculation.
9663-domnei-a-comedy-of-woman-worship:
James Branch Cabell wrote Domnei, a Comedy of Woman-Worship, in 1920, a romance of knights and ladies in Poictesme. Domnei, Cabell explains from troubadour lore, names a knight's service to his lady, proving love to merit love. Perion, unmasked and gay, woos Melicent, while a bishop aids him and Demetrios schemes. Parts follow Perion, Melicent, and Demetrios in turn.

Chapters trace wooing, wedding, oversea quests, and a final conquest, as love tests honor and wit. Cabell's prose stays ornate, ironic, and musical. A reader gets a rich medieval fantasy of love's service, half romance and half jest, from Cabell's invented province.
a-cathedral-courtship:
Kate Douglas Wiggin sends young Katharine Schuyler touring the cathedral towns of England with her aunt Celia, in a tale first published in London in 1893, as this edition's title page shows. Katharine writes the story herself in letters and diary notes, beginning at Winchester in May. Aunt Celia means to improve her mind; a young architect keeps crossing their path.

Winchester, Salisbury, Wells, and other cathedral cities pass in turn, with services, climbs, and teas between. The courtship grows quietly under the sightseeing, opposed by plans made for Katharine at home. Wiggin mixes travel notes with gentle romance, and the book became a favorite gift volume of its day.
adventures-in-friendship: David Grayson reflects on friendship as a lived practice, through neighbours, strangers, and old acquaintances met on the road and at home. Essays on fraternity, bread shared at table, and belonging show how small acts of kindness build lasting bonds. The tone is warm and unhurried, treating friendship less as an idea than as daily conduct, open doors, and time given freely.
astral-worship:
J. H. Hill, a medical doctor, wrote this study of ancient religion around one bold claim: the gods of old were the sun, planets, and stars in disguise. His contents lay out an earth-centred cosmos of firmament, zodiac, and constellations, then read sacred numbers seven and twelve as keys to myth. A twelve-thousand-year cycle frames the system's history.

Chapters name the sun as God Sol and retell the fall and redemption of man as a seasonal story. Feasts get solar readings throughout: the Nativity, Lent, Passion Week, Easter, and Michaelmas become anniversaries of the sun's yearly course. Hercules' twelve labours, hours, months, and seasons all join the pattern, making the book a full statement of nineteenth-century solar-myth theory.
bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-church-o:
A. Hugh Fisher wrote this description of Hereford Cathedral and its see for Bell's series, published by George Bell and Sons in 1898. The series' general preface states the bargain plainly: monographs accurate and well illustrated at a popular price. Each writer aims at enough scholarship for the student of archaeology and history, without language too technical for the ordinary visitor or tourist. A photochrom view of Hereford from the Wye fronts the volume.

Local benefactors speak in the text through old rhyme. One inscription thanks a man through whom all people may freely come and go. No custom, toll, or other woe is charged. His godly wife Anne enlarged the gift of house and land. The country is bound to pray for them, the verse insists, or else it were to blame. Fisher mixes such records with the fabric's measured history.
britannica-1911-animal-worship:
Animal worship is an ill-defined term. It covers a very wide range of facts. At one end stands the true divine animal. Worshippers conceive it as a god-body. At the other end sits mere respect. Even respectful names for animals fall under it. Bones of slain animals may receive honour too. The entry warns about its sources. Travellers' reports on Africa often prove unreliable.

Classification proceeds in two ways. Outward form gives one scheme. Inward meaning gives another. Whole species may be sacred together. Alternatively, one fixed animal may be sacred. The entry thinks species worship came first. Individual cults developed from it later. Chieftainship and annual sacrifice drove that change. Syncretism, the blending of cults, also contributed. Egyptian bull worship anchors the closing references. Ethnology reports supply further cases.
britannica-1911-apprenticeship:
Apprenticeship is a contract in which a master binds himself to teach a trade, explains a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The learner, called the apprentice, in turn serves the master for a set time. The word comes from a French term that means to learn.

Roman law says nothing on such a contract, the entry notes. The practice seems to have arisen in the middle ages. It formed a core part of the trade gild system. Gilds sought to shield skilled workers from feudal lords. They also held sole rights to practise their arts in set places. A gild body held both masters, who could teach and practise, and apprentices, who were still learning.
britannica-1911-benjamin-judah-philip:
Judah Philip Benjamin (1811–1884) was an Anglo-American lawyer born a British subject at St Thomas in the West Indies. His parents settled at Charleston, and he left Yale without a degree to enter a New Orleans attorney’s office. Admitted to the bar in 1832, he built a strong practice with John Slidell.

Louisiana sent Benjamin to the United States Senate in 1852, and he declined a supreme court judgeship to stay in politics. In 1861 he joined Jefferson Davis’s Confederate government, serving as attorney-general, then secretary for war, then chief secretary of state. After the war he rebuilt his life at the English bar, where his book on sales law became the standard text.
britannica-1911-blois-countship:
Blois is the subject of a countship article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The countship of Blois was held in fee from 865 to about 940 by the margraves of Neustria. Robert the Strong and his heirs held it in that period. Near 940 it passed to a new family of counts. That family held it for near three centuries.

The article says the new counts were at first very powerful. They joined the countship of Touraine to Blois for a long span. They also held Chartres for long periods. The line of counts called the Theobalds began near 940. One count, Odo the Second, was among the most warlike barons of his time. He joined a kinsman's lands to his own. He died in 1037 while fighting in Lorraine. Later counts took part in the first crusade and held lands in Troyes as well.
britannica-1911-cluwer-philip:
Cluwer, Philip (1580–1623), also spelled Cluver, Cluvier or Cluverius, was a German geographer and historian, born at Danzig in 1580. After travel in Germany and Poland, where he learned Polish, he began law at Leiden but soon turned to history and geography under Joseph Scaliger. Campaigning in Bohemia and Hungary, imprisonment and travel in England, Scotland and France filled his middle years. He finally settled in Holland, receiving a regular pension from Leiden Academy after 1616.

He began to publish his works in 1611, the entry records, and died at Leiden in 1623. Principal writings are Germania Antiqua in 1616 and Siciliae Antiquae with Sardinia et Corsica Antiqua in 1619. Two works appeared after his death, Italia Antiqua in 1624 and Introductio in Universam Geographiam in 1629. Ancient lands, Germany, Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and Italy, form the map of his scholarship as listed here.
britannica-1911-francis-sir-philip:
Sir Philip Francis (1740-1818), English politician and pamphlet writer, was born in Dublin on 22 October 1740. His father, Dr Philip Francis, was known for translations of Horace and other classical authors. The son held clerkships from boyhood, served on missions abroad, and wrote for the London press while still a government official.

Francis is named here as the supposed author of the Letters of Junius, printed from 1769 to 1772. In 1773 he joined the new supreme council of Bengal and reached Calcutta the next year. His long feud with Governor-General Warren Hastings led to a duel in 1780 in which he was badly wounded. Home again, he entered parliament and kept pressing the case against Hastings until his death in 1818.
britannica-1911-hip: Hip is a short word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica covering two senses of one spelling. In the first sense the hip is the part formed by the top of the thigh bone and the side of the pelvis. In four-legged animals the same part is generally called the haunch. In the second sense a hip is the fruit of the dog rose. The article notes that hips are usually named together with haws, the fruit of the hawthorn.
britannica-1911-image-worship:
Image worship is weighed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica through a sharp opening contrast. Two people may kneel side by side before a statue. Their outward acts look the same. Yet what each thinks the image is can differ by a wide gap.

One may see a mere picture of a higher being, with no power of its own. It is like a photo of a loved one hung on a wall, prized as a picture and no more. The other may see a living home for the god, full of divine force. The Latin Church by rule teaches the first view for its people. Sacred images there should show the story of Jesus, the Virgin, and the saints to those who cannot read.
britannica-1911-massinger-philip:
Philip Massinger, an English playwright, is traced in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was baptised at Salisbury in 1583, son of a gentleman. His father served in parliament and in a great lord's household. The young Massinger entered St Alban Hall, Oxford, in 1602. He left in 1606 with no degree, his father now dead.

Massinger went to London to live by the stage and plays. For years he wrote with other playwrights and stayed in the shade. The Virgin Martyr of 1621 first bore his name with Dekker's. A joint plea for help from Massinger and two fellow writers shows the strain. The plea sought aid from the manager of their company.
britannica-1911-neri-philip:
Philip Neri, an Italian churchman who lived from 1515 to 1595, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Florence, the youngest child of a lawyer of that city. His early teaching came from the friars at San Marco, the famed Dominican house there.

At about sixteen a fire destroyed nearly all his father's property. Philip was sent to a childless uncle, a merchant at San Germano, to help in his business. The hope was that he might inherit the man's wealth, and he won his trust and love in full. The plan failed only because Philip resolved to take holy orders instead. In 1533 he left for Rome, where he tutored in a Florentine household. There he began his work among the sick and poor, which later won him the name Apostle of Rome.
britannica-1911-schaff-philip:
Philip Schaff, an American theologian and church historian who lived from 1819 to 1893, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Chur, Switzerland, in January 1819, he was taught at Stuttgart and at Tübingen, Halle, and Berlin. Teachers such as Neander shaped him most. In 1842 he became a lecturer at Berlin. In 1843 he was called to a chair of church history in Pennsylvania.

On his way he spent six months in England and met Pusey and other Tractarians. His inaugural address of 1844 held that Romanism and Protestantism were stages in one appointed development of the Church. That view aroused fierce opposition. He was tried for heresy in 1845 and found not guilty, and opposition soon died out.
britannica-1911-scrip:
Scrip, in strict use, is any writ document. The word is a worn form of script, from a Latin verb for to write. It may owe its shape to a like word for a pilgrims bag. In trade use it takes a far more tight sense. The 1911 Britannica entry sets that sense out in full.

Scrip there is a note put out by a public firm. It is put out when the price of shares is paid in parts at set dates. It holds when the full sum has not yet been called up. The writ gives the man named the right to be held as taker of the shares. It can pass from hand to hand. When all calls are paid, its holder may claim the full share proof. The word is oft used in loose speech for shares as a whole.
britannica-1911-serpent-worship:
Snake worship across the world is mapped in a faith entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Proof of its weight comes from all parts of the wide earth. India still holds the cult in strength in the present day. A census count showed tens of thousands of snake votaries there. Naga worshippers and Guga's flock both ran to vast rolls of names.

Old and mid-age Indian books back that count of the cult. Stone shrines at Sanchi and Amravati show snake gods in adoration pose. High faiths keep old crude roots in their rites, the entry argues. That law holds from Babylon and Crete to Greece and Peru. Myths and folk scraps from both worlds tell the same tale. Like sights work on like minds in like ways, it holds.
britannica-1911-sidney-sir-philip:
Sir Philip Sidney was an English poet, court man, and soldier who lived from fifteen fifty-four to fifteen eighty-six. He was born at Penshurst, the son of a lord who ruled Ireland three times. His youth was spent at home, then at school with his life long friend Greville. At Oxford he made more fast friends.

A match with the child of a great lord was planned, then broke off. Leave came to roam abroad to learn new tongues. He went to Paris with a lords train and was there in the days of the great slaying of the faith. That sight fed his zeal for his own creed.
britannica-1911-skippon-philip:
Philip Skippon, an English soldier of the Civil Wars who died in 1660, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at West Lexham in Norfolk, he took up soldiering young. In 1622 he served with Sir Horace Vere in the Palatinate. He fought in most of the battles and sieges of the Low Countries. He was wounded at Breda in 1625 and again in 1637.

Skippon returned to England in 1639 as a veteran of wide experience and took a command in the Honourable Artillery Company. As war neared in 1642, he was made commander of the City troops. He rode the lines at Turnham Green, cheering his raw militia. Essex made him major-general, in charge of the foot. He stood out at the first battle of Newbury. At Lostwithiel in 1644, deserted by Essex, he had to surrender.
britannica-1911-stubbs-philip:
Philip Stubbs, an English pamphlet writer born near 1555, is the subject of a brief 1911 Britannica article. He studied at Cambridge and then at Oxford but took no degree. He spent most of his time in travel about the country. He began to write near 1581 and died near 1610.

His chief work, The Anatomie of Abuses, came out in 1583. It was a fierce attack on the manners, dress, games, and habits of his day. The piece notes it is still prized for the rich detail it gives on those topics. In 1591 he printed A Christal Glass for Christian Women. That book called for at least seven print runs. More works of a devout kind followed.
britannica-1911-tulip:
Tulip, the genus Tulipa, is described in a botanical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tulips are bulbous herbs of the lily family. They grow wild from the Mediterranean shores across Asia as far as Japan. The cup-shaped flowers have six segments in two rows and six free stamens.

The fruit is a dry, leathery capsule holding many seeds. Kinds are told apart by traits such as whether the bulb scales are woolly or smooth inside. Garden tulips have been crossed so often that their wild types are now hard to trace. The article names source kinds for prized strains, among them a Caspian kind behind the early Van Thol tulips. A yellow wild kind found in England is treated as a doubtful native there.
britannica-1911-wouwerman-philip:
Philip Wouwerman, a Dutch painter of battle and hunting scenes who lived from 1619 to 1668, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Haarlem, he learned the first steps of his art from his father, a history painter of moderate skill. He then studied with Jan Wynants, a painter of landscapes.

Back in Haarlem, Wouwerman joined the painters' guild in 1642 and died there in 1668. Catalogues have listed 800, then more than 1200, pictures under his name. Many of those, the entry warns, are most likely the work of his two brothers or of his many imitators. His true works show great spirit and wide variety. They return again and again to cavalry battles, military camps, cavalcades and hunting parties. He is praised alike for his lively figures, his skilful animals and his fitting landscape grounds. His style changed across three periods of his art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-wor:
An entry on Christian worship, the homage paid to God, to Christ, to saints, and to things closely linked with God. Worship comes from the Saxon word for honour, the Latin cultus, and in its widest sense it covers hero worship, emperor worship, and devotion to angels, relics, and the Cross. This article treats Christian worship in its proper sense.

Degrees of worship matter most. Worship offered straight to God is latria, adoration due to God alone, since giving it to a creature would be idolatry. Worship of martyrs, angels, and saints is dulia, a lower, dependent honour for God's servants. The Virgin holds a rank apart, so her worship is hyperdulia. Even relics and images share in this dependent honour through their link with holy persons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devil-worship:
An entry on devil worship, a pairing the writer calls hard to credit yet plainly real across ages and races. Worship and tribute work alike: subjects serve a just king gladly, but also pay blackmail to a pirate chief to buy off feared harm. Rude polytheism held both kinds at once, honouring kind gods in love while propitiating dreaded powers.

That fear-bought service, the entry argues, unlocks much of the puzzle, from African medicine men to medieval magicians. It also warns against a crueller error at home: crowds of innocent people were put to death on witchcraft charges. Quoting Augustine, it closes by suggesting that slander and cruelty can outdo any dark rite as devil worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-disparity-of-:
Disparity of worship is a bar to marriage set up by the Church to guard the sanctity of the sacrament. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that a Catholic may not marry a person unfit to receive the sacrament. That unfitness may lie in never having received baptism, the door to the other sacraments, or in denying that marriage is a sacrament at all.

It may also lie in denying the unity or lifelong bond of marriage, or in holding views that imperil the three ends and blessings of wedlock. The bar thus covers all who stand outside the Catholic faith and worship. The entry then works through the law in detail, a long study of how the Church shields marriage from unions that cannot bear its full meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-partnership:
Partnership means an unincorporated group of two or more persons, called partners, carrying on some set occupation together for profit, with profits shared among them. Lindley traces partner to part, to divide or share, and notes that co-partnership in the loose sense of co-ownership is now obsolete. English common law might still count an association a partnership even if profits served ends beyond the partners' own use.

Roman law treated partnership at length as societas, a consensual contract needing no form or writing, effective by bare consent. Archaeologists find it highly developed in ancient Babylon. Later pages sort its kinds, formation, partners' powers and liabilities, dissolution, and the canon-law questions it raises for clerics and religious, with English and Roman rules set side by side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-relationship:
Relationship, carnal and spiritual, is the theologians' term for a connection between persons set up by nature or by civil or canon law. Three kinds are distinguished: natural, legal, and spiritual, though legal relationship lies outside this entry. Natural or carnal relationship springs from carnal intercourse of man and woman, marital or not, and takes two forms, consanguinity, blood kinship, and affinity, kinship by marriage.

Spiritual relationship comes from church law and attaches to Baptism and Confirmation. It runs between minister and recipient, and also between sponsors on one side and the recipient and his parents on the other. Under the discipline of the day it bars marriage between the persons named, acting as a diriment impediment, a barrier that makes a marriage invalid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-philli:
Robert Phillip was a Scottish priest who served as confessor to Queen Henrietta Maria in the troubled years before the Civil War. Ordained at Rome, he returned to Scotland in 1612. Betrayed by his own father and seized while saying Mass, he was tried at Edinburgh as a seminary priest in September 1613. His death sentence was commuted to banishment.

In France he joined the Oratory founded by Cardinal de Berulle. In 1628 he went to England as the queen's confessor. At her request he sought papal money against the king's enemies. When the talks were exposed he was impeached as a papal spy who had tried to pervert Prince Charles. Proceedings dropped after Richelieu objected to his name appearing. Phillip was later sent to the Tower for refusing the Anglican Bible oath in 1641. Freed through the queen, he followed her to The Hague and Paris, where he died in 1647.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-islip:
Simon Islip, Archbishop of Canterbury, was born at Islip near Oxford and died at Mayfield, Sussex, on 26 April 1366. Schooled at Oxford, he took doctorates in canon and civil law and was elected Fellow of Merton in 1307. His gifts as an ecclesiastical lawyer won him many benefices. He held the rectory of Easton, then exchanged it in 1332 for the archdeaconry of Stow, which he kept a single year, and held Horncastle rectory besides.

Bishop Burghersh of Lincoln, then treasurer and Chancellor of England, made him a Lincoln prebendary in 1327, and he held prebends in succession before becoming vicar-general in 1337. In London he entered royal service as a chaplain, and Edward III trusted him in diplomacy and politics, giving him wide powers during the king's absence in France in 1346. After plague claimed two successors to Canterbury, Islip was chosen archbishop in 1349 and ruled until his death.
chess-and-checkers-the-way-to-mastership:
Edward Lasker's Chess and Checkers: The Way to Mastership, printed in New York in 1918, teaches both games in one volume. Lasker promises complete instructions for the beginner and valuable suggestions for the advanced player. His preface notes that the world war had given chess great impetus. Prison camps, field hospitals, and trenches all played.

Part one covers chess: rules, elementary tactics, and the relative value of the pieces. General principles of strategy treat pawn openings and the middle game. Two illustrative games include Lasker against Capablanca at New York in 1915. Part two gives checkers the same treatment, with its five fundamental positions. Problems close each part. The book's diagrams appear as text drawings in this edition, and its tone is brisk, clear, and encouraging to learners.
doe-osti-17047520-evaluation-of-ethanol-:
Robert McCormick and Nimal Naser of the National Laboratory of the Rockies evaluated ethanol as a marine fuel in this September 2026 report. The work was written for Growth Energy under a work for others agreement. Shipping needs lower carbon fuels, and ethanol is a widely made alcohol fuel. The study weighs ethanol against both standard marine fuels and other green options.

Sections cover world shipping fuel rules, the coming IMO net zero framework, fuel storage and bunkering, spill behavior, and air pollutant emissions. Engine chapters ask how ethanol burns in marine engines and what changes ships would need. Safety guidance for alcohol fuels from the IMO is reviewed as part of the picture.
doe-osti-2584727-cog-software-architectu:
Livermore document LLNL-TR-2006166, by Edward M. Lent in May 2025, is the software architecture design description for COG. COG is the laboratory's Monte Carlo radiation transport code, used in nuclear criticality safety. Architecture documents exist so a code outliving its authors stays maintainable. This one records the design for version COG 11.3. Its revision line reaches back to 2009, and to COG 11.1 in 2014.

Contents follow the genre: purpose, scope, and references, then requirements and objectives. The design section inventories the main code modules, and the rest alphabetically. It lays out the code's operational phases, with flow diagrams phase by phase. Approval rests with the Nuclear Criticality Safety Division. For a code whose answers decide whether fissile material setups are safe, the architecture record is part of the safety case itself. This update keeps that record current with the software as it now stands.
doe-osti-3012259-human-factors-considera:
Human factors questions raised by autonomous advanced reactors are mapped in an Idaho National Laboratory report, INL/RPT-25-89289. The authors are Katya Le Blanc, Casey Kovesdi, Anna Hall, Ronald Boring, and Tina Miyake. NRC coauthors Niav Hughes Green and Stephanie Morrow joined them. The landscape analysis reviews public material on anticipated designs. Its purpose is to show where NRC review guidance may need updating.

Nine reactor concepts were characterised by design and concept of operations against level of autonomy. Simple designs with passive safety need fewer operator actions, which may support higher automation. The Kairos KP-FHR pebble bed concept illustrates the pattern. Its safety functions need no active systems or manual action.
doe-osti-3374043-effect-of-magnetic-hyst:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229828-2026-TECH, dated June 2026, is by Harshita Singh with Boris Podobedov. It looks at how magnetic hysteresis in magnet steel affects the dipole field of the Electron-Ion Collider's Rapid Cycling Synchrotron. The ring's magnets ramp up and down once per second, and the steel's memory of past fields can leave errors in the field the beam sees. Field quality matters because the ring must hold beam losses low and keep polarization intact.

The note reviews hysteresis and the Barkhausen effect, the jumps in magnetization as domain walls move. It notes that steels processed for accelerator magnets give off little Barkhausen noise. One cited test put the noise peak near one two-thousandth of the main signal. That was at a peak field of 0.4 tesla. Work on the effect in accelerator magnets is scarce, which the note treats as a sign the impact is small.
doe-osti-3376627-solar-training-and-educ:
A final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-EE0010824, submitted October 17, 2025, closes Solar Landscape's STEP-UP training program. Kevin Finley is the contact of record. STEP-UP stands for Solar Training and Education Partnership for Underserved Populations. The firm trained solar installers in tandem with community groups in several U.S. regions. Each region got a plan shaped by local job checks and the firm's own field experts.

The report argues the timing is right. Solar work is growing fast in states like Illinois. State data cited there count 5,975 solar jobs since 2023, with growth of 5.7 percent in 2023 alone. Installation and project work hold the largest share, at 3,478 jobs. Utility funds add a further push: one cited pool pays out thirty million dollars in three ten-million steps. Trainees from underserved areas stand first in line for that work under the program's design.
doe-osti-3377902-clean-cities-and-commun:
The Clean Cities and Communities Partnership 2024 Activity Report, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5400-98656 from June 2026, accounts for a year of coalition work on cleaner transportation. Five authors are printed: Mark Singer, Caley Johnson, Alana Wilson, Lauren Reichelt, and Muhammad Abdullah. Local coalitions run events, working groups, and training to move fleets and drivers toward cleaner fuels and vehicles.

The activity tables count reach across the network. Coalition-organized events drew 441 participants in one category, with 66 percent of coalitions taking part, and workforce and technical training reached the highest participation rate at 84 percent. Across all counted activity types, the report totals 1,127 activities with 672 coalition involvements. Stakeholder working groups, tailored expertise, and project funding help make up the rest of the year's work.
doe-osti-3398696-energy-technology-innov:
An Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project deck dated April 7, 2026 introduces technical assistance for St. Vincent's House in Galveston, Texas. Mike Campton of the National Laboratory of the Rockies is the regional lead and presenter. The technical team comes from Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. It includes environmental engineer Molly Grear and systems engineers Kasey Johnston and Jacob Garbe. Regional partners come from STEM NOLA and the Southeast Sustainability Directors Network.

The opening slides explain the program the project rides on. ETIPP helps coastal, remote, and island towns build energy systems that cost less, run more reliably, and stay more secure. It pairs Department of Energy funding with four national labs and nine regional partners. More than 80 communities take part. The help spans strategic planning, generation, efficiency, and energy modeling. Grid and regulation topics are covered too. Here it is applied to one Galveston community institution.
doe-osti-3484812-energy-technology-innov:
Dated August 2026, report NLR/TP-5R00-100447 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies sets a strategic energy plan for Washington County, Maine. Neah Downs Dybas of the Rockies lab wrote with Brenna Cohen and Amber Blum of the Island Institute. The plan grew from the Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project.

The core idea is relational infrastructure: trust and coordination alongside wires. About two thirds of local outages stem from causes beyond full utility control. Two priority areas target that outage risk first. A third builds utility-community coordination. Rural counties get a plan that treats people and poles as one system.
domnei-a-comedy-of-woman-worship:
James Branch Cabell set his 1920 romance Domnei in the age of troubadours, and he calls it a comedy of woman-worship. The word domnei, a note at the front explains, named a knight's whole service to his lady: the deeds, habits, and hopes by which he strove to earn her love. The tale is told in four parts named for its chief figures.

Perion, a masked knight, serves the lady Melicent, who weds another and then seeks oversea when he is taken. The Greek prince Demetrios enters, amused at first, then a wooer himself, and at last a captive of the code he mocked. Swords, songs, and sieges fill the chapters, each titled with an old ballad turn: how Perion was unmasked, how the sword Flamberge was lost. Cabell writes courtly love as both high game and gentle joke.
for-auld-lang-syne-a-book-of-friendship:
Ray Woodward's For Auld Lang Syne is a book of friendship, gathering what various writers have said about that world-wide bond. Woodward dedicates the selections to his father, Fred E. Woodward, and argues that friendship stays the same bond at heart, whether it joins people of intellect or people with no sense of mission.

Its manifestations differ, Woodward notes, but friends in both cases are drawn close and united by a bond written about throughout the ages. No single volume could gather all that has been written on friendship, so Woodward presents selections that show its varied forms. Readers who enjoy anthologies of wise and tender writing will find this a warm companion.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDisciplining:
A United Press article dated September 21, 1978 reports testimony before the House assassinations committee. Retired FBI inspector James H. Gale told the committee that the Bureau had secretly disciplined seventeen supervisors and inspectors. Their failure: they had not listed Lee Harvey Oswald as a national security risk before President Kennedy was killed.

Secret discipline meant the public never learned of the punishment at the time. Gale's testimony brought it out fifteen years later, during a fresh congressional inquiry. The article preserves that admission, a rare public sign that the Bureau itself judged its Oswald handling a failure.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TapesOwnership_: Richard Nixon gave sworn testimony after leaving the presidency, and the New York Times printed excerpts in August 1975. The questioning concerned the White House tapes and who owned them. Nixon's answers mattered because the tapes had driven the Watergate scandal and his resignation a year earlier. The excerpts let readers hear the former president defend his claims in a legal setting, under oath.
nasa-tm-19700029981-methods-for-nasa-uni:
A NASA task group on university relationships prepared this report in July 1970. NASA headquarters in Washington issued it. From its first days, the agency had drawn on universities for parts of the space program.

The report is a catalog, with commentary, of the methods NASA uses with universities. It also lists methods the agency and its centers could reasonably use. The ties run to administrators, faculties, and students alike. NASA asked for the survey as it tried to help strengthen the schools. In return, the schools added depth and skill to the national space effort.
nonsenseorship:
G. G. Putnam and others wrote Nonsenseorship, a set of sundry observations on prohibitions, inhibitions, and illegalities. G. P. Putnam edited the book, and Ralph Barton drew the pictures. Contributors include Heywood Brown, Ben Hecht, Dorothy Parker, and Alexander Woollcott. Frank Swinnerton and Wallace Irwin also appear.

The opening piece, We Have With Us Today, starts with bootleg prices. Good whisky costs less, it notes, than a banned book from a booklegger. A group of not too serious thinkers were asked for their views on pet prohibitions. No one of puritan leanings, the editor admits, was invited. Prohibition era America is mocked in essay after essay.
plague-ship:
Andre Norton, writing as Andrew North, published the science fiction novel Plague Ship in 1956. Its hero is Dane Thorson, cargo-master-apprentice aboard the Solar Queen. The ship is a Galactic Free Trader spacer with Terra registry. Dane serves under Captain Van, alongside assistant astrogator Rip Shannon.

Chapter one, headed Perfumed Planet, finds Dane in the ship's cramped bath cabin. Rip works scented paste into his back. The crew is landing on Sargol, whose people, the Salariki, will not talk business with a Terran who does not smell right. They can also talk for hours without giving a straight answer. Dane doubts the venture and says it holds a galaxy of ifs. Rip insists they will come out credit-happy if it works.
play-making-a-manual-of-craftsmanship:
William Archer's Play-Making: A Manual of Craftsmanship was published in London in 1912. Archer was a well-known theatre critic, and the book is his guide to how a play is built. He says in his opening note that the text is almost wholly new, and that his examples come from plays a student can read and check.

Early chapters take up the choice of a theme and the line between what is dramatic and what is not. Later parts turn to the daily routine of writing a play. Archer draws many of his lessons from Shakespeare and Ibsen, and the book is dedicated to Brander Matthews.
the-banner-boy-scouts-or-the-struggle-fo:
George A. Warren's scout story was copyrighted in 1912 and printed in the United States by Cupples and Leon. A meeting in a barn opens the contents, followed by a chapter on what it means to be a Boy Scout. Disappearing coins raise a puzzle early on.

The first scout leader is chosen, a coward is checked, and a boy named Peleg sets a trap that later turns against him. Rival troops appear, a fire breaks out, and a boy named Jack gets his chance. Headings such as Well Done, My Boy suggest tests of character as much as outdoor skill in this boys' series book.
the-blood-ship:
Norman Springer wrote a sea tale published by Grosset and Dunlap in a third edition, after a 1922 copyright by W. J. Watt. Chapter one says a talkative writer drew the story out of Captain Shreve. The writer came aboard that morning with an agent's letter, meaning to sail with the crew.

Weak lungs and a search for mild tropical air are his excuses; his real aim is King Waldon, a dead Samoan trader. He has heard Shreve knew Waldon, the island adventurer who sailed into a Samoan harbour in an open boat with his beautiful young wife, from nowhere. Shreve's yarn promises a bloody past behind that legend.
the-ghost-ship:
Richard Middleton wrote The Ghost-Ship as the title tale of a set of ghost stories, most first placed in journals like The Century and Vanity Fair. A villager of Fairfield tells the tale.

The teller grants that strangers call Fairfield pretty, while its folk find it plain but home. Fairfield, he claims, is the ghostiest place in all England. Ghost lads dead in war meet their girls on the green, ghost hounds hunt in packs, and a headless man sits by the well at noon while children play at his feet. The tale to come, he warns, was queer even for Fairfield, where the dead are part of daily life.
the-high-school-boys-fishing-trip:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The High School Boys' Fishing Trip, subtitled Dick & Co. in the Wilderness. The contents list chapters such as Tom Reade Has a Brand-New One, Dick & Co. Driven Up a Tree, Stalling the Red Smattach, The Box That Set Them Guessing, and The Scream That Started a Race. Chapter one opens on a warm night at a street corner.

Tom Reade, described as an amiable senior at Gridley High School, stops to wipe his face and neck and greets Timmy Finbrink. Timmy grants that the night is middling warm, though the heat does not seem to trouble him much. Hancock sets a summer outing tone before the wilderness trip begins.
the-manual-of-heraldry-fifth-edition-bei:
The Manual of Heraldry, in its fifth edition from Arthur Hall, Virtue and Company of London, promises a concise description of the terms of heraldry. It offers a dictionary of every designation in the science, illustrated by four hundred engravings on wood. Chapter one, on the origin of coats of arms, defines its subject first: heraldry teaches how armorial bearings and their accessories are blazoned, that is, set out in proper terms. The author declines to chase the exact period when heraldry began. Many volumes, he notes, have been written on its origin and on the antiquity of single charges in a shield, and an elementary work gains little from that inquiry.

In all ages and countries, he observes, men emerging from barbarism to civilization have used figures of living things as marks. The manual teaches a symbolic language through its dictionary and plates.
the-otterbein-hymnal-for-use-in-public-a: The Otterbein Hymnal was prepared by Edmund S. Lorenz for use in public and social worship, and published at Dayton, Ohio, in 1892 by the United Brethren Publishing House. The Church of the United Brethren in Christ had ordered a small hymnal for general church purposes in 1886. Only the front matter is present here, so the hymns themselves do not appear. The pages name the advisory committee on music and letters, and a table of contents begins but is cut off.
the-phantom-ship: Captain Frederick Marryat wrote The Phantom Ship, shown here in a London printing dated in roman numerals 1896. The title page and a bare contents list are all that is present, so the novel itself does not appear. The list names thirty-seven chapters by number alone, with no titles. A second record carries the same 1896 title page but a shorter contents list, and a third record, labeled part 2, carries the opening chapter instead.
tom-swift-and-his-airship:
Victor Appleton opens Tom Swift and His Airship with an explosion chapter in a laboratory. Tom stands ready by complicated apparatus while Mr. Sharp, a dark, nervous man, leans over a large tank and warns him to look out. Sharp is about to turn on the gas, unsure what may happen.

Contents promise a trial trip, colliding with a tower, getting off a roof, a runaway auto, and the Red Cloud departing. Later chapters bring robbery charges, a wreck, a sheriff aboard, and a raid. Readers get a boys' airship adventure that begins with a risky gas experiment.
tom-swift-in-captivity-or-a-daring-escap: A Daring Escape by Airship is promised in the Tom Swift in captivity story by Victor Appleton, presented through twenty-five chapter headings. A strange request and a circus man open the book, and Tom decides to go despite warnings about a rival. Fire on board and a narrow escape follow. Later headings bring a wild horse stampede, a native battle, giant land, a king's palace, captives held, and weak giants. Chapter one is announced without text following. The contents list alone is given in this record.
tom-swift-in-the-caves-of-ice-or-the-wre: Victor Appleton's Tom Swift in the Caves of Ice, or the Wreck of the Airship, is presented through twenty-five chapter headings. Andy Foger's triplane, a stolen map, and grave suspicions start the rivalry. Chapter one opens with Eradicate asking whether Tom will fly again today, and Tom planning a trip to Waterford to call on Mr. Damon, then breaks off. Later headings promise musk oxen, ice caves, a gold valley, a wreck, and rescue. The contents and that opening exchange are what is present here.
victorian-short-stories-stories-of-court:
Victorian Short Stories: Stories of Courtship gathers five tales of lovers. Angela, an inverted love story by William Schwenk Gilbert, leads the book. Anthony Trollope adds The Parson's Daughter of Oxney Colne. Hubert Crackanthorpe, George Egerton, and Israel Zangwill complete the set. Gilbert's tale is noted as first printed in The Century Magazine in September 1890.

His narrator is a poor paralysed man. For six years he has lived in one small room over a side canal in Venice. A deaf old woman tends him and makes his bed. He lives on some thirty pounds a year from watercolor drawings of flowers and fruit, sold in London through a friend. He describes his window with care. It stands five feet above the canal water, and the house juts out above it. That odd room drives his tale. Courtship here comes inverted indeed, watched from a sickbed.
